titleStmt.title: Tractatus septiformis de moralitatibus rerum, Book 3: On Birds

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise auto-generee (IA, non relue par un latiniste) a partir du texte latin du corpus zoomathia sous zoo65/1l (Marcus de Urbe Veteri, Tractatus septiformis de moralitatibus rerum). Seul le livre 3, "Tractatus 3: De avibus" (oiseaux, 41 chapitres, 1377 citations), est traduit ici et integralement preserve div par div (oeuvre > section1 livre [n=3] > section2 chapitre > cit avec <bibl> d'attribution et <quote>). Les livres 4 "Tractatus 4: De piscibus" (poissons, 493 citations) et 5 "Tractatus 5: De animalibus" (animaux terrestres, 2061 citations) restent a traduire lors d'une session ulterieure. Recueil homiletique de similitudines animalieres (bestiaire moralise a l'usage des predicateurs), chaque chapitre associant une ou plusieurs autorites citees (Aristote, Pline, Isidore, peres de l'Eglise, Ecriture) a une exemplification tiree du monde animal, appliquee aux vices et vertus. Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un latiniste avant toute citation savante. Correspond au texte latin deja present dans le corpus sous zoo65/1l (source Sourcencyme/IRHT).

cit.quote: The eagle is found to have these conditions, or properties.
First, as Isidore and Pliny say, it holds the principate among birds, like a queen.
It signifies the Blessed Virgin, lady and queen of the angels and of all good spirits. Esther 10: 'Esther is the one the king wished to have as his wife, and wished to be queen.'
Hence the Church sings in the Sequence: 'the joys of the supernal Mother; there the queen of virgins, surpassing the height of the ranks.'
Second, as Isidore says, it flies higher than all other birds, and is borne on a motionless wing above the air and above the seas.

It signifies that the Blessed Virgin has surpassed all the choirs of angels and of the blessed in dignity and in seat, with a perfect triumph over the world, the flesh, and the devil. Ecclesiasticus 24: 'I have had the primacy in every nation, and in every land, and among every people; I have, by my own virtue, trodden down the necks of the proud and the exalted.'
Hence the Church sings: 'the holy Mother of God is exalted above the choirs of angels to the heavenly kingdom'; and again: 'you who today, glorious, triumph with the angels.'
Isidore: it gazes at the sun in its own orb without its eyes being dazzled.

It signifies that the Blessed Virgin contemplates clearly the source of eternal light and the abyss of wisdom. Ecclesiasticus 24: 'I am the mother of fair love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope.'
'The cherub'; and it flew, it flew upon the wings of the wind.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: The cherub, that is, the fullness of knowledge, above which the Blessed Virgin ascends by eternal contemplation and by particular possession; but by the name of the winds of the wings are understood the angels, or the souls of the saints, according to Gregory in the Moralia, above whom the Blessed Virgin rises in knowledge.

Fourth, as Pliny says, among all birds it is the most generous: for the prey it seizes, unless it is burning with excessive hunger, it does not eat alone, but rather exposes it, as it were, in common to the birds following it, once it has taken its own portion; and so other birds are accustomed to follow the eagle, hoping that some portion should be given to them from its prey.
It signifies the Blessed Virgin, generously prepared, as far as lies in her, to pour out the gifts of her munificence, from the glory she has attained, upon all souls.

Hence she herself says, Ecclesiasticus 24: 'come over to me, all you that desire me, and be filled with my fruits; for my spirit is sweet above honey, and my inheritance above honey and the honeycomb.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Homilie 'super missus est' sive In laudibus Virginis matris Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'In dangers, in straits, in doubtful matters, think of Mary, call upon Mary. Let her not depart from your mouth, let her not depart from your heart, and, that you may obtain the help of her prayer, do not depart from the example of her conduct. For following her, you do not go astray, and, asking her, you do not despair.'

Fifth, as the same Pliny says, it places in its nest two precious stones called 'echedes,' of which one is male, the other female, without which, it says, it cannot give birth. It also places in its nest the gem called 'achates,' to guard its chicks from the venomous bite of reptiles and from harmful thunder.

It signifies that, by the example of the Blessed Virgin, whoever wishes to perform works of perfection ought first to place it in his own affection, in resolve — just as the Blessed Mary did before she conceived or bore Christ, as is found in Luke 1; and Bernard attests: virginity, and humility, and, third, a preserving safeguard of works against temptations and dangers, holy prayer.
Or the two precepts of charity, with grace, or preserving faith. Matthew 22: 'on these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets.'
Romans 7: 'who shall deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord.'
Romans 5: 'being justified by faith, let us have peace with God, through this grace in which we stand, and let us glory in the hope of the sons of God.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, Regula tertia vel Preceptum Augustini

cit.quote: Augustine, at the beginning of his Rule: 'before all things, my brothers, let God be loved, then the neighbor, since these are the precepts specially given to us.'
As the Gloss says, on Matthew 24: 'it has the keenest sense of smell; for it perceives carcasses across the sea.'

So, by the example of the Blessed Mary, every holy and devout soul ought always to perceive the fragrance of heavenly pastures and consolations. Ecclesiasticus 24: 'I have given forth a sweet odor like the finest myrrh, and as sweet balm not mixed.'
Blessed John the Evangelist said, speaking to God at the end of his life: 'your fragrance, Lord Jesus, has stirred up eternal desires in me.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs, and elsewhere: 'whoever does not perceive your fragrance, O good Jesus, is either dead or foul-smelling.'
7. Seventh, as Pliny says, all animals of another species, even birds of prey, are terrified at its sight and hearing; hence hawks and similar birds scarcely hunt by day, when they hear an eagle.

It signifies that demons are put to flight and terrified at the invocation and remembrance of the Blessed Virgin and of God's saints. Ecclesiasticus 24: 'I have trodden down, by my virtue, the necks of the proud and the exalted; my memory is unto everlasting generations.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'the very garments of Paul were a terror to demons.'
Eighth, as Ambrose says in the Hexameron, it is renewed by the heat of the sun, its feathers shaken and singed, and by afterward plunging into a living spring.
For, as Augustine and Pliny say, in its old age it suffers a dimness of the eyes and a heaviness of the wings.

It signifies a holy man always renewing himself, above the mind's level, toward spiritual things, and casting off and shaking off, through fiery devotion and heavenly grace, his daily failings and vices. 2 Corinthians 4: 'though our outward man is corrupted, yet our inward man is renewed day by day.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, De ecclesiastica hierarchia Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Dionysius, in the book On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy: 'it is the property of virtue to progress always and continually.'

Ninth, as Isidore says, 'the eagle (aquila) is so named from the sharpness (acumen) of its eyes.' For its sight is said to be of such and so clear a keenness that, because of its being raised so far above the earth, it can scarcely be seen by human gaze, and yet it sees little fish swimming in the sea, and, descending like a stone, seizes the fish, and so drags its captured prey to the shore.

It signifies the keenness of perception that ought to be in a prelate, for the zeal of drawing souls from the sea of this world to the harbor of salvation. 2 Corinthians 2: 'let us not be deceived by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his devices.'
Likewise, 2 Corinthians 12: 'most gladly will I spend, and be spent myself, for your souls.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie in Hiezechielem Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, on Ezekiel: 'nothing pleases God so much as zeal for souls.'
Ambrose: it is a bird naturally hot and dry, stronger and bolder than the strength of other birds, whose strength is greatest chiefly in its wings, feet, and beak.

It signifies holy men, glowing with the grace of the Holy Spirit and dried out from the desire of the world, being especially strong to contemplate, be moved, and speak ardently and effectively of God and concerning God. 2 Corinthians 3: 'where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. But we all, beholding the glory of the Lord with open face, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot know divine things.'

Eleventh, as Ambrose says, and Aristotle too, in book 9: there is a certain kind of eagle, called 'almachor,' which hangs its chicks up by the talon before the rays of the sun, and compels them to look at the sun, even before their wings are fully grown, and for this purpose strikes them, and turns them toward the sight of the sun. And if the eye of one waters, it either kills it as a degenerate offspring, or casts it out of the nest. But if it sees it gaze steadily at the ray of the sun, it loves it, and nurtures it, as being, by nature, like itself.

It signifies that prelates ought to know God, and ought to instruct their subjects to know God and divine things, and ought to cast out from the fellowship of the Church those who refuse to know him. Galatians 4: 'my little children, of whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you.'
Dionysius: 'a priest lacking illumination falls from his rank.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: As Gregory says in the Moralia: although it gazes at the brightness of the sun with unflinching face, it nonetheless directs and inclines itself toward the sight of prey and of things below. It signifies that men raised up by contemplation ought to provide for the building up and the aid of the weak, and to condescend to them.

Hence, in a mystery of this, on the ladder of Jacob, Genesis 28, the angels are said first to ascend and afterward to descend, since the good man, and especially the prelate, following Christ's example, ought by night to spend the night with Christ on the mountain of contemplation, but by day come down to build up his brothers and condescend to the weak. Psalm 91: 'to declare your mercy in the morning, and your truth in the night.'

It is written of blessed Francis that 'it was the way of that angelic man never to be idle from good, but, like the angelic spirits on Jacob's ladder, now to ascend to God through contemplation, now to bend down to his neighbor through condescension.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: As Gregory says in the Moralia, it nests on the highest crags, where it rests safe from every hostile attack, and yet, once it has seen a carcass or the prey it desires, it suddenly makes for the depths.

It signifies men established by God on the height of contemplation, or of heavenly conduct, nonetheless condescending for the sake of the grace of souls' salvation — following the example of blessed John the Evangelist, who, though he was always wholly active upward toward God, nonetheless condescended even to seeking out the robber in the forest, and bringing him back into the Church, as indeed he did. 1 Corinthians 9: 'whereas I was free from all men, I made myself the servant of all, that I might gain the more.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'as though Paul were the common father of the whole world, so did he run about for all, and hasten to gather and bring all into the kingdom of God.'

As Aristotle says in book 6, the eagle lays at most three eggs, but casts the third out of the nest, since it broods too heavily upon them. And he adds that at that time it is weakened so much that it cannot hunt well for its young's food, since then its talons curve and its wings whiten, and it is then greatly burdened in giving food to its chicks.
It signifies that a cleric ought to be content with two common benefices, and yield the third, if he has one.

And this very thing, if he must do it, greatly troubles and weakens him in spirit, since he cannot hunt for more benefices, and so he cuts back his alms and interposes the duties of piety. Ecclesiasticus 14: 'the eye of the covetous is insatiable in his portion of iniquity; he will not be satisfied till he consume his own soul, drying it up; and there will be sorrow to him over his own table. And even if he does well, he does it unknowingly and unwillingly, and in the end he shows forth his malice.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Epistola Hieronymi ad Paulinum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, to Paulinus the priest: 'to the believer, the whole world is a wealth of riches; to the unbeliever, even an obol is wanting.'

Fifteenth, as the same Aristotle says, the eagle, casting its now-grown chicks from the nest, gradually urges them to fly, and makes them hungry, so that they follow it more eagerly through the air for the sake of food. And if perhaps they are slow to leave, it strikes them with its beak, and withholds their food, so as to compel them to leave. And once they are complete in strength and in feathers, it drives them from itself, and is no longer solicitous over them.

It signifies that prelates ought, by words and examples, to urge their subjects toward heavenly things, and ought to punish the lazy, and those unwilling to advance or labor for their salvation, but may let go those already instructed and complete in virtue. Deuteronomy 32: 'as the eagle enticing her young to fly, and hovering over them, spreads her wings, and has taken them, and carried them on her shoulders.'
Dionysius, in his reply to Architeca: 'great kindness and great piety befit the highest priests.'
'I have become all things to all men, that I might save all.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Sixteenth, as Gregory touches on in the Moralia: when the chicks are newly born, being too weak to take and digest coarser food, it draws in and sucks the blood and thinner moisture of its prey into its own mouth, and vomits up what it has drawn in into the mouths of its chicks, and so restores them with lighter food, until they grow strong enough to take stronger food.

It signifies that an abbot, or prelate, or even a preacher, ought to give simple teachings to the simple. 1 Corinthians 3: 'as unto little ones in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not meat; for you were not yet able.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, De ecclesiastica hierarchia Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Dionysius, in the book On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy: 'it is dangerous to wish to unlock the sacred mysteries to the weak and the unclean.'

As Aristotle says in book 6, there is a certain kind of eagle, which he says is called 'achat,' which cares for its young for a long time, and, when the chicks fly, flies with them, and gives them food, and sometimes hovers over them, taking care of them, ready to resist other birds, should they happen to gather to harm or injure its chicks in any way.

It signifies that abbots ought to be at labor with their subjects, and take care of them, and defend them from evil attacks. Ecclesiasticus 32: 'they have made you a ruler; be not lifted up, but be among them as one of them. Have a care for them, that you may receive the crown of grace, and win the esteem of the assembly.'

It is written of Julius Caesar, in the Historia Tripartita, that he did not say to his soldiers 'Go,' but 'Come,' whenever something had to be done for the good of the state. On account of which all followed him, and loved him affectionately.
The eagle's gall is highly medicinal: for, put into eye-salves, it sharpens the sight, and relieves dimness and other troubles of the eyes.

It signifies that anger, through zeal, in a holy prelate or teacher, is beneficial to those who stray from the way of truth, or to others ignorant or slothful. 1 Timothy 1: 'of whom is Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: Bernard, book 1 On Consideration: 'it is fitting to be impatient with vices.'
Nineteenth, as Aristotle says in book 16, the eagle is a bird exceeding in heat and dryness, and so it is bold and wrathful, since strong anger exists only in bodies of great dryness.
It signifies those who are noble by nature, and yet bold and wrathful through vice. Ecclesiasticus 27: 'anger and fury are both of them abominable, and the sinful man shall be subject to them.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Liber de precepto et dispensatione Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Against which Bernard, On Dispensation and Precept: 'scandal is not to be remedied by scandal.'
And Proverbs 3: 'lean not upon your own prudence.'
And 1 Corinthians 8: 'take heed lest perhaps this your liberty become a stumbling-block to the weak.'

Twentieth, as the same Aristotle says, in book 4, the eagle is hostile and an enemy to innocent birds: for it seizes them with its talons, and strikes them with its beak, and terrifies them with its roaring voice.

It signifies, by the lion, certain oppressors of the innocent and the poor, and threateners of their inferiors, raging against them in a bestial way — against which, Ecclesiasticus 4: 'be not as a lion in your house, terrifying your own household, and oppressing those under you.'
The Gloss, on the Psalm 'O God, come to my assistance': 'it is great savagery to persecute the poor, as Judas persecuted Christ.'
The eagle fears the vulture, and especially that species of eagle that dwells in, or only around, water, which is called 'amachel.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: It signifies that demons, dwelling in wantonness and petulance, are terrified by Christ, who, according to Gregory, on Job 28: 'descends from on high, like a vulture, to take upon himself the human race, made, as it were, a corpse through sin.'
'The demons believe, and tremble.'
'When the unclean spirit is gone out of a man, he walks through dry and waterless places, seeking rest, and finds none.'

bibl.author: Beda Venerabilis, Expositio Bede in Marci Evangelium

cit.quote: 'The devil.'

Twenty-second, as Pliny says, the eagle has one foot closed like a goose's foot, with which it steers itself in the water when it is accustomed to descend near its prey; but it has the other foot divided, with the sharpest talons, with which it seizes its prey.

It signifies the cunning, the snares, and the rapacity of demons, and especially of usurers. Proverbs 28: 'he that deceives the just in a wicked way shall fall into his own ruin, and the upright shall possess his goods. He that heaps together riches by usury and loan gathers them for him that will be bountiful to the poor.'

bibl.author: Iohannes Chrysostomus, Homilie super Mattheum Iohannis Chrysostomi

cit.quote: Chrysostom, homily 47 on Matthew: 'if you wish to see the soul of a lover of gold, you will find it like a garment pierced through everywhere by ten thousand worms, and rotten, and full of rust.'

Twenty-third, as the same Pliny records, the eagle's feather has a certain hidden corrosive power. Hence he says that an eagle's feather placed among the feathers of other birds destroys and corrodes them, just as strings made from wolves' intestines, placed in a fiddle or a lyre together with strings made from sheep's intestines, destroy and ruin them.
It signifies those whose malice infects and corrupts others, by example, or by word, or by association. 1 Corinthians 5: 'know you not that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?'
'He that touches pitch shall be defiled by it, and he that has fellowship with the proud shall put on pride.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, to Nepotian the priest: 'keep such companions that you are not brought into ill repute by their company.'
Twenty-fourth, as Aristotle says in book 1, the eagle does not love company, but rather flees it. For it is not possible for birds that have joined talons to be among the company of others.

It signifies solitary, or fierce, men who do not agree with their own multitude in a gathering. Ecclesiastes 4: 'woe to him that is alone, for when he falls he has none to lift him up. And if two sleep together, they shall warm one another; how shall one alone be warmed?'
Augustine, in the book of Confessions: 'every part that does not agree with its whole is disgraceful.'
As Pliny says, the eagle trains its young for the hunting of other birds, and drives them to it by striking and wounding them with its beak.

It signifies usurers and robbers, instructing and forcing their children to imitate their own crimes and evil deeds — against which, Ecclesiasticus 7: 'have you children? Instruct them, and bow down their neck from their childhood. Have you daughters? Take care of their body.'
Charlemagne, as it is written in the Historia Tripartita, who had his sons and daughters raised in the most honorable manner.
Twenty-sixth, as Aristotle says, it is unnatural against its own children, reckoning them strangers, casting them from itself, when their sight is closed against the sun.

It signifies worldly men, who love only those like themselves, intent on the world's prosperity. John 7: 'the world cannot hate you; but me it hates, because I give testimony of it, that its works are evil.'
Bernard, in a certain letter: 'I wish you to be a friend of the poor, but still more an imitator of them. The former is the rank of those advancing; the latter, of the perfect.'
The hawk is found, according to the authorities, to have these conditions, or properties.
For first, as Isidore says, it is a royal bird, armed more with spirit than with talons, and what nature denies it in bodily size, it makes up for in strength and boldness of spirit.

It signifies the spiritual boldness and strength in a man's soul that is of God, such as Paul had for the house of the Lord. 2 Corinthians 10: 'let such a one think this, that such as we are in word by letters, being absent, such also we will be indeed, being present.'
'Paul was bold, and, as it were, always girded for battle, plotting a certain fire of war.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, it is a bird devoted to catching other birds, and from this seizing and preying, the hawk ('accipiter') is called 'raptor.'
It signifies those who are strongly zealous for drawing souls to Christ. 2 Corinthians 12: 'most gladly will I spend, and be spent myself, for your souls.'
It is said in the legend of blessed Sebastian that this saint led to heaven souls that the devil was trying to carry off.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie in Hiezechielem Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, on Ezekiel: 'zeal for the converting of souls is greatly pleasing to God.'
Third, as Boethius says, hawks are, in a marvelous way, solicitous about rousing and driving their small, and now flight-capable, young to seek out food, lest, once grown, they become slothful.

They signify the lazy and idle, who must be driven to labor by their prelates and superiors. 2 Thessalonians, the last chapter: 'we have heard that there are some among you who walk disorderly, working not at all, but curiously meddling. Now these we command and beseech, in the Lord Jesus Christ, that, working with silence, they eat their own bread. And if any man will not work, neither let him eat.'
It is asked: why did Aegisthus become an adulterer? The cause is at hand: he was idle.
Bernard and Gregory alike, in various places: 'on the way of God, not to advance is to fall back.'

Fourth, as Bede and Ambrose say, among hawks some are predators of the air only, others of the land only, just as with eagles. The first kind seize only flying birds; the second, however, strike and attack them as they sit on the ground.

They signify contemplative and active men, in their various ways seeking and finding their own spiritual food or refreshment — following the example of Mary and Martha, as is found in the mystery of Luke 10.

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, De verbis domini Pseudo Augustini
De assumptione sancte Marie Virginis Paschasii Radberti

cit.quote: And Augustine relates this very thing in the book On the Words of the Lord, and it is also read, or found, in a homily On the Assumption of the Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin.
Fifth, as Aristotle says in book 14: the hawk is a hot and dry bird, its bulk of flesh reduced, adorned with a variety of plumage and feathers.

It signifies the religious man, glowing with the love of God and dried out from desire for the world, honorable in his senses and gracious in his conduct. 2 Corinthians 6: 'in all things let us exhibit ourselves as the ministers of God, in charity, in chastity, in sweetness, in the Holy Spirit, by the armor of justice on the right hand and on the left, as having nothing, and possessing all things.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, De officiis ministrorum Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Ambrose, in the book On the Duties of Ministers: 'riches provide no help toward a blessed life.'
Which the Lord clearly showed in the Gospel, when he said: 'woe to you rich,' and 'blessed are the poor, for theirs is the kingdom of God.'

Sixth, as the same Aristotle says, now it ascends into the air with the greatest agility and speed, so much so that it withdraws itself from the sight of men, now suddenly plunges downward upon its prey.

It signifies the holy man, free from the world, now driving himself upward to contemplate God, now condescending to save or build up his neighbor, now ascending and descending Jacob's ladder, as is found in that sacred mystery, Genesis 28.

It is written of blessed Francis that, following Christ's example, he was accustomed to go out onto the mountain to pray and to spend the night with Christ, but by day to come down to build up his brothers and refresh them in Christ.
Of blessed Bernard too, this same thing is written, in almost every respect, according to the sentences.

Seventh, as Aristotle says in book 14: the breast of the hawk is very sharp, yet furnished with only a little flesh, and the sharper it is, the better its flight, since if it had a very broad breast it would stir much air and its motion would be labored. It has flesh, however, since what is sharp is weak unless it has a covering of sufficient flesh to suit its fittingness.

It signifies that the sharpness of sacred diligence, or of holy Scripture, together with the depth of poverty, is most effective for actions raised above the mind toward God, and for salutary conferences with one's neighbor. 1 Corinthians 2: 'now we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is of God, that we may know the things that are given us from God; which things also we speak, not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the showing of the Spirit and power.'
'I shall be found young and sharp'; and before it, in chapter 7: 'for in her is the spirit of understanding, holy, sharp,' and so on.

Augustine, in the book of Confessions: 'set with my mother, at the mouth of the Tiber, we were talking together, alone, most sweetly. And we were reaching out, with the mouth of the heart, together toward the supernal streams of the fountain of life. And we touched the region of unfailing abundance, and our minds passed beyond, where you feed Israel forever with the food of truth, in the pleasantness of your ever-green paradise.'
Its greatest strength is in its breast, its talons, and its beak, with which it at once attacks and pierces the brain of its prey.

It signifies that spiritual strength exists in a holy soul through a heart magnified toward God, through strict abstinence, and through the boldness and effectiveness of evangelical zeal. 2 Corinthians 10: 'the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty, through God, unto the pulling down of fortifications, destroying counsels, and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every understanding unto the obedience of Christ, and having in readiness to revenge all disobedience.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie in Hiezechielem Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, on Ezekiel: 'nothing so pleases God as zeal for souls.'

Ninth, as the author says, taking it from Pliny: its gall is medicinal, and is beneficially mixed into eye-salves; for it sharpens the sight, and destroys and consumes the white spots on the eyes; and its dung does the same.

It signifies that the bitterness and humility of penance are very effective for the cleansing, or clarifying, of spiritual or inward darkness; hence Ephesians 5 says, to one lying in mortal sins: 'rise, you that sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, De vera et falsa penitentia Pseudo Augustini

cit.quote: Augustine, On Penance: 'penance is a certain best and perfect thing, calling back every failing to perfection.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Tenth, as blessed Gregory says, on Job: in old age, when it feels itself weighed down by the burden of its feathers, it spreads its wings against the sun's rays, the south wind blowing. And so, from the sudden blowing wind and the melting heat of the sun, its pores are opened, and, once opened, it shakes off its wings, and so the old feathers fall out, and new plumage, or feathers, grow back; and so the newness of its feathers makes it fitter for hunting.

It signifies, in one entering religious life, the putting off of the old man and the putting on of the new, through the mediation of grace and charity. Ephesians 4: 'put off, therefore, the old man, and be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who, according to God, is created in justice and holiness of truth.'

bibl.author: Leo Magnus, Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: Pope Leo, in a sermon On the Circumcision: 'awaken, then, O man, and recognize the dignity of your nature, which, although it was deformed in Adam, has nonetheless been reformed in Christ.'

Eleventh, as the author says, it requires a very well-ordered diet: for if it eats too much, it is of no use for the hunt; if too little, it becomes weak; but if in a middle measure, it then rightly performs its office.

It signifies that, in a religious man who wishes duly to triumph over his enemies and rationally to do what he ought, a discreet abstinence is called for. Romans 12: 'that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, your reasonable service' — that is, let your abstinence be discreet.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the first homily On Several Martyrs: 'for although we owe strictness to vices, we owe compassion to nature.'

...of hawks: for one kind is domestic, and one kind wild. The domestic kind catches wild birds, and carries them to its master, and gives them up; but the wild kind seizes domestic birds. They signify the diversity of preachers in the Church. For some are domestic, like the prelates of churches, who, as it were by office and by their own nature, catch rebellious men, restraining them even by ecclesiastical censure, and bringing them back to the bosom of the Church, and delivering them to Christ the Lord.

Some are wild, like religious, who, in a penitential habit, by commission, preach to the household of the faith in familiarity, and so call them, snatching them from the fire of avarice, of pride, and of lust, and the other vices of this age. 1 Corinthians 3: 'what, then, is Paul? And what is Apollo? The ministers of him whom you have believed, and to every one as the Lord has given. I have planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the increase. Now every man shall receive his own reward, according to his own labor.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: But alas, since Gregory says, in his homily On the Evangelists: 'behold, the whole world is full of priests, and yet there are few who thrust the Lord's harvest onto the threshing-floor.'

Thirteenth, as Aristotle says in book 14: it is of a proud and indignant nature. For if, by some mischance, it does not seize the prey it has attacked, it scarcely returns to its master's hand that day.

It signifies those who, being of a great heart, disdain when they cannot fulfill what they desire, or when what they wish for does not come to pass — or prelates who do not proceed according to what is advised them, and, deflated by this, turn aside, and sometimes cause uprisings. Proverbs 29: 'he that is easily moved to indignation shall be more prone to sins.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Epistola Hieronymi ad Letam de institutione filie

cit.quote: Jerome, to Laeta, On the Education of a Daughter: 'for it is easier to be a follower of evils, and to imitate the vices of those whose virtues you cannot attain.'
'The mind of man is prone to evil,' and so on.
Fourteenth, as Bede says, hawks are especially harmed by smoke.
It signifies that preachers are especially harmed by vainglory, which puffs them up. Isaiah 10: 'it shall be wrapped up in the pride of smoke.'
But holy Lucy the virgin did not do this. And likewise blessed Cecilia; for she said to the tyrant: 'your wisdom and your knowledge labor in smoke' — as if to say, 'not mine.'
As the same Aristotle says, as long as they live and are good at hunting, they are loved by their masters.
It signifies good and useful servants and officials, dear to their masters as long as they act usefully and virtuously. Proverbs 17: 'a wise servant shall rule over foolish sons.'
'If you have a good servant, let him be dear to you as your own soul; treat him as a brother,' and so on.

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: An example is found in blessed Martin, who, as is found in his Life, in turn served his one good servant to such a degree, and so on.
The osprey, or falcon, is found, according to our authorities, to have these conditions, or properties.

For first, as the Gloss on Deuteronomy 14 says, where it is named, it is the same as the falcon; others, however, say otherwise. Whatever it may be, it is a bird greedy for prey, and very bold: for it attacks birds far larger than itself, striking and assaulting them with breast and feet.

It signifies presumptuous men, daring and attacking more than they ought, against the pattern of Scripture. Proverbs 23: 'set a bound to your prudence'; and in the same book, chapter 3: 'lean not upon your own prudence.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: Paul separated John, who was called Mark, from his company, since he was too much given to boldness.
Second, as the author says, there is a small kind of osprey that catches other, tiny birds.
'The osprey has scant strength of body. There are also birds that are its very smallest prey and food.'

It signifies bailiffs and petty officials, greedy, or lesser officials of every kind, oppressors and attackers of the poor and the lowly. Proverbs 28: 'a poor man that oppresses the poor is like a violent shower, which brings a famine.'
The continuous Gloss: since such a shower comes with force, and quickly passes, and does much harm, so too is such a lord, or bailiff, or evil prelate.
Geese have these properties, according to blessed Ambrose, in the Hexameron, book 5, chapter 21.

For, to use his own words there: 'who would not marvel at the nightly watches of geese, which attest to their vigils even by the constancy of their cries? Indeed, by this the Roman Capitol was saved from the Gallic enemy. Rightly do you owe it to them, Rome, that you reign. Your gods were sleeping, and the geese were watching. And so, on those days, you sacrifice to the goose, and not to Jupiter. For your gods yield to the geese, by whom they know themselves to have been defended, lest they too be captured by the enemy.'

Blessed Ambrose adds further that these birds seem to have their first kinship with fish, since they too, in like manner, delight in the use and gift of swimming, raising themselves up with the oarage of their wings, and going forward, with their tail as a rudder, into deeper water.

As to the first, they signify prelates and evangelical preachers, in times of the Church's tribulations and persecutions, tirelessly setting themselves, for the salvation and defense or protection of souls, against strong prayers and exhortations, following the example of the Apostle. 2 Corinthians 12: 'most gladly will I spend, and be spent myself, for your souls.'
Wisdom 18: 'the man in haste, without complaint, brought forth a shield, and, pleading prayer, resisted wrath, and put an end to the necessity.'
Chrysostom, On Paul: 'Paul was bitten, torn apart, afflicted, when he saw his children perishing. And he reckoned tyrants to be, as it were, mere gnats.'

As to the second, it signifies these same men, in the world's storms and their own dangers or temptations, knowing how to escape by raising and spreading out their eternal desires, and by having a firm and steadfast perseverance in their resolves, following the Apostle's pattern: 'in all these things we overcome, because of him that has loved us.'

An example is found in blessed Lawrence and Vincent, who, conducting themselves loftily in their passion, and possessing the habit of perseverance, took no heed of their tyrants' torments, and so, triumphing over all things, passed happily to the heavenly harbor, as is found in the accounts of their passions.
The owl is found, from the accounts of naturalists, to have these conditions, or properties.
A gloomy bird, laden with feathers, but held back by heavy sloth.

It signifies those clinging solitarily to themselves, held fast by private love, by deep sloth and the slackness of continual negligence, to whom applies that saying, Jeremiah 48: 'cursed is he who does the work of God negligently'; against which, Proverbs 28: 'he that tills his land shall be satisfied with bread; but he that follows idleness is most foolish.'
Bernard and Gregory alike, in many places: 'on the way of God, not to advance is to fall back.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, it is weak in flight.
Job 24: 'they have been rebellious to the light; they have not known his ways, nor have they returned by his paths.'
Ambrose: 'feigned fairness is not fairness, but a twofold iniquity.'
Isidore: it lingers, day and night, in tombs, or in the hollows of abandoned buildings.
It signifies evil men, whose works are hidden, and whose life is dark. John 3: 'every one that does evil hates the light, and comes not to the light, that his works may not be reproved.'
Ephesians 5: 'for the things that are done by them in secret, it is shameful even to speak of.'
Bede, on Paul: 'the wicked always seek out hiding places, and hide themselves from the sight of the saints.'
Fourth, as the same Isidore says, it is said among augurs always to portend evil, for, seen in a city, they claim it signals desolation.

It signifies that, on account of heretics and false brothers, the world is to be destroyed, and is sometimes destroyed. Baruch 4: 'I have been left desolate by many, because of the sins of my children, who have turned away from the law of God; let no one rejoice over me, a widow and desolate.'
Hence it is said, Proverbs 29: 'when the wicked are multiplied, crimes shall be multiplied; but the just shall see their downfall.'
The Gloss, on Matthew 12: 'heretical depravity casts down to the depths of every evil.'
Fifth, as Aristotle says in book 8, it sees more clearly by night than by day.

It signifies that evil men are, in their own way, more perceptive, or more shrewd, toward evil and in evil deeds, than good men are toward good and in good deeds. Luke 16: 'the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light.' And an example is given of mice, which are more resourceful by night than larger and better animals are by day, at seeking food for themselves.

...the jackdaw, a bird of the crow's kind. For this eats the owl's eggs by day, when the owl does not see well at midday, and it is then stronger than the owl; but the owl eats the jackdaw's eggs by night, when the jackdaw does not see, and the owl is then stronger.

These things signify that demons are refreshed by the deeds of hypocrites, and hypocrites by the suggestions of demons. Proverbs 2: 'who are glad when they have done evil, and rejoice in most wicked things, whose ways are perverse, and their steps infamous.'

Blessed Jerome, in the Lives of the Fathers, gives an example of a holy father who saw demons exulting, when the brothers spoke wanton words with mirth, and went about among them in the manner of pigs.
...birds flit around it, as though out of contempt or mockery, and pluck out its feathers; and this is the reason by which fowlers catch birds with it and by means of it.

This signifies that good men detest and shudder at evil men, according to the counsel of the wise man, Proverbs 4: 'delight not in the paths of the wicked, and let not the way of evil men please you.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus, Epistole Senece ad Lucilium

cit.quote: Seneca, to Lucilius: 'the first step of innocence is to hate wicked things.'
And the Canon: 'not to disturb the perverse, when you are able, is nothing other than to nourish them.'
Eighth, as Isidore says, its frequent hooting at night is, according to the conjecture of augurs, a portent of someone's death nearby.
It signifies that the impatient laments of evil men, in a time of adversity, are a sign, or a messenger, of eternal death for themselves and for their imitators.

Which is clear from the example of Cain, Genesis 4, and the example of Esau, Genesis 27. Proverbs 19: 'he that is impatient shall suffer damage'; against which the verse: 'patience is a noble kind of conquering,' and so on.
Ninth, as Aristotle says, it feeds on dung and other filth.
It signifies wanton and lustful men, wasted and defiled by their own lusts, according to that saying of Joel 2: 'the beasts of burden have rotted in their own dung.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'for beasts of burden to rot in their own dung is for carnal men to end their life in the stench of lust.'
Tenth, as Isidore says, it is held in hatred by the other birds.
It signifies that the devil is held in hatred, even by God, and by the angels and saints. Wisdom 14: 'the wicked man, and his wickedness, are hated by God alike.'
'There was, then, a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: David always advancing, and growing stronger and stronger, but the house of Saul decreasing daily.'
He who, when he can, does not cease to oppose an open crime is not free from the suspicion of secret complicity.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, De viris illustribus Hieronymi

cit.quote: Blessed Jerome wrote, in the book On Illustrious Men, that blessed John the Evangelist once met, with his disciples, the heresiarch Marcion, who said to John, 'do you know us?', to which John replied: 'I know the firstborn of the devil.'

Likewise it is said in the Gloss on 2 John, and it is in the canon of the Decretals, that when John was bathing with his companions in the baths, and Cerinthus, another heresiarch, arrived, he said: 'let us flee from here, lest the very baths in which Cerinthus, the enemy of truth, wishes to bathe, collapse upon us.'
'Oil.'

It signifies those who secretly plunder the goods of churches. Ephesians 5: 'have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness; for the things that are done by them in secret, it is shameful even to speak of.'
For indeed one who is dark within always seeks hiding places without, as is suggested in John 3.
'Birds.'

It signifies hypocrites, showing themselves zealous for piety, and virtue, and truth, while being nothing of the kind. Titus 1: 'they profess that they know God, but in their works they deny him, being abominable, and unbelieving, and to every good work reprobate.'

bibl.author: Passio sancti Tiburtii (in passione sancti Sebastiani)

cit.quote: An example is found in Torquatus, in the legend of Saint Tiburtius, who long pretended to be a Christian, and finally betrayed blessed Tiburtius.
As the same author says, when it is attacked by birds, it turns itself on its back, and defends itself with beak and feet.

It signifies that evil men defend and protect themselves against the good with all their effort, in words and deeds, as is clear from the example of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, Numbers 16; and 2 Timothy 3: 'now as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith.'
Likewise, an example is found in Simon Magus, who resisted Peter forcefully, and was at last confounded.
...it hunts and eats mice and bats, and roams and flies about by night; but by day it hides itself in the crevices of walls.
It signifies demons hunting and feeding on unclean things, and their movements in darkness. Psalm 81: 'they walk on in darkness; all the foundations of the earth shall be moved.'
'But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.'

bibl.author: Iohannes Damascenus, De fide orthodoxa Iohannis Damasceni

cit.quote: Damascene, in his little book: 'every malice and every uncleanness were devised by the devil.'
Doves are found, according to the authorities, to have these conditions, or properties.
For first, as the Gloss on Song of Songs 1 says, on that verse 'your eyes are as doves': 'it lacks gall, and does not wound with its beak' — except, sometimes, its own mate, out of familiar boldness.

It signifies a man patient in all things and toward all. Song of Songs 1: 'behold, you are fair, my love, behold, you are fair, your eyes are doves' eyes; the beams of our houses are of cedar, our rafters of cypress.'
'I was like a meek lamb, that is carried to be a victim'; Ecclesiasticus 3: 'my son, do your works in meekness, and you shall be beloved above the glory of men.'
Augustine, to Proba: 'a man ought to take more care not to lose his patience than to lose any other thing.'

Second, as is found in the same place, it nests in the clefts of the rocks, and there gathers and shelters itself in dangers, as another Gloss on Song of Songs 5 says, on that verse 'your eyes are as doves, beside the streams of waters.'

It signifies that, in the wounds of Christ, the dove of the holy soul ought to dwell, by transformation, and gather itself there from the storm of the world. Song of Songs 2: 'arise, my love, my beautiful one, my dove, in the clefts of the rock.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'Christ willingly dwells with the soul that willingly meditates on his passion.'
'Leave the cities, and dwell in the rock, you inhabitants of Moab, and be like a dove that makes her nest in the mouth of a hole above.'
'Its young.'

It signifies men of whom Job 29 speaks: 'I was the father of the poor, I was an eye to the blind, and a foot to the lame; the blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow.'
Augustine, in his sermons, and elsewhere: 'I have never seen a compassionate man come to a bad end.'
Fourth, as the same Gloss says, it gathers and brings together other stray doves.
It signifies Job 31: 'if I have despised him that was passing by, because he had not clothing; if the stranger did not lodge outside, if my door was open to the traveler.'
Blessed Paul the first hermit, who received blessed Anthony, when he came to him wandering, with the greatest charity, as blessed Jerome relates in his Life.
Fifth, as the same Gloss says, it stays most gladly and diligently near flowing water.

It signifies those given, by affection, to the sacred Scriptures, to the tears of devotion, and to the inflowings of grace. Psalm 1: 'he shall meditate on his law day and night; and he shall be like a tree that is planted near the running waters, which shall bring forth its fruit in due season.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, Tractatus Augustini in Iohannis Evangelium

cit.quote: Augustine, On John the Evangelist: 'he drank the streams of the Gospel from the very sacred fountain of the Lord's own breast.'
'Doves upon the streams of waters, that are washed with milk, and dwell beside the fullest streams.'

Bernard, in a certain sermon: 'the sons of the prophets too, whom, as Jerome says, we read to have been monks in the Old Testament, withdrew to the secrecy of solitude, dwelling in huts by the streams of the Jordan. John the Baptist, too, knew no dangers or death for as long as he dwelt and lived in the desert.'
As the same Gloss says, it chooses the better and purer kinds.

It signifies that, for those who wish to be saved, the teachings and examples of the best ought to be preferred above all. 2 Peter 1: 'for we have not, by following artificial fables, made known to you the power and presence of our Lord Jesus Christ.'
'I count all things to be but loss, for the excellent knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord.' Philippians 3.
James, at the end: 'take, my brothers, for an example of suffering evil, and of longsuffering, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.'
Jerome, in the prologue to the Pentateuch: 'what, then? Do we condemn the ancients? By no means!' But I prefer the apostles above them all.
Seventh, as the same Gloss says, it has a groan instead of a song.
It signifies one not seeking consolation in this world, but always sighing and groaning for the other. Isaiah: 'we shall roar all of us like bears, and, like doves, meditating, we shall mourn.'
'Like the young of the swallow, so will I cry, and I will meditate like a dove; my eyes are weakened, looking upward on high.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, Epistola Augustini ad Probam

cit.quote: Augustine, to Proba: 'every soul in this world ought to reckon itself desolate and wretched'; and he adds: 'in the riches of this world there can be no true consolation.'
It flies in flocks, and loves company.

It signifies a good soul, willingly joining itself to holy men, or religious persons. Ecclesiasticus 4: 'be affable to the congregation of the poor'; likewise, chapter 6: 'stand in the multitude of prudent elders, and join yourself from your heart to their wisdom.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, Epistola Augustini ad Probam

cit.quote: Augustine, to Proba: 'let good men be present, by whom sorrows of every kind are soothed and lightened.'
Ninth, as the same Gloss says, it defends itself with wings and beak.

It signifies that holy men arm themselves against tempters and temptations with heavenly desires, with actions of the mind raised on high, and with the words of sacred Scripture. Ephesians 6: 'put on the armor of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day; take up the helmet of salvation and the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God.'
Origen: 'the words of sacred Scripture are more powerful than any poisoned enchanter's songs.'
Tenth, as is found in the same Gloss, it does not accept carcasses or other unclean things.

It signifies that a man who is in charity wishes to be refreshed and to delight in nothing but clean and religious works. 1 Thessalonians 4: 'for God has not called us unto uncleanness, but unto sanctification.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, On the Love of God: 'for holy men, all flesh is an instrument of good work.'
Eleventh, as is found in the same Gloss, it feeds its young.

It signifies a man cherishing and cultivating the two precepts of charity, and wholly occupied and intent on them: 'on these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets'; 'do this, and you shall live.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, Regula tertia vel Preceptum Augustini

cit.quote: Augustine, at the beginning of his Rule: 'before all things, my brothers, let God be loved, then the neighbor, since these are the precepts especially given to us.'

'Her eyes are as doves upon the streams of waters': 'sitting by the streams, she watches for the shadow of the hawk coming from afar, and, as soon as she sees it, flees into the depths of the hole, and hides herself; there too she protects and defends herself from the heat.'

It signifies the soul of a religious man, diligently intent on the speculation, or consideration, of the sacred Scriptures, in which and through which, knowing the cunning of temptations and the hostile wickedness around him, he takes refuge in inward things, through prayer and sacred meditation, to preserve and protect himself; or even, as was touched on above, in the wounds and torments of the crucified Christ.

Hence, on that verse of Song of Songs 2, 'come into the clefts of the rock,' Bernard says, in a certain sermon: 'the dove in the cleft of the rock' is safe from the hawk and from the heat, since the just man, placed in the wounds of Christ through the memory of his passion, is protected by it from the snares of demons, and is refreshed from the burning heat of vices.

Hence Origen says, On the Passion of Christ: 'so great is the power of diligent meditation on the passion of Christ, that, if it is continually held in memory, no desire, no temptation of sin or of demons, can overcome it, but at its presence the whole army of sin and death is put to flight.'
As Constantine says in the Viaticum, its blood is medicinal.

For it is said that its blood, drawn warm from under the right wing and put or dropped into the eyes, soothes pain and heals ophthalmia of the eyes. It signifies that the blood of the Lord's passion, coming forth from his right side, cleanses, if fiery devotion is present, every darkness, or blindness, of guilt and ignorance from the soul. Hebrews 9: 'the blood of Christ will cleanse our conscience from dead works, to serve the living God.'
'O abundant redemption before God, since it was not a drop of blood, but a flood, that flowed out through five parts of the body.'
It has burning dung, which it casts out of the nest, and is accustomed to teach its young to cast it out too.

It signifies that the evangelical man ought entirely to shake off from himself, with his whole affection, the desire he has contracted, or love of earthly things, and, as far as he can, urge others of the household of the faith to do the same, by example and exhortation. Philippians 3: 'I have counted all things as loss, and I esteem them as dung, that I may gain Christ.'

Blessed Eugenia said, as is found in her acts, to Melania, a most wealthy citizen who offered her riches, if she — believing her to be a man — would consent to unite with her: 'let those like you keep your wealth; it delights us to beg with Christ.'

Something similar, and stronger, blessed Agnes said to the prefect's son: 'depart from me, food of death, for I am already forestalled by another lover,' and so on: 'he has set a mark upon my face, that I should admit no other lover but him.'

Blessed Ambrose also relates, in book 3 On Holy Virginity, that there was a certain young man of such great love for holy chastity that, feeling women drawn to him because of the beauty of his face, he cut his lips with a knife and disfigured himself, so that no woman could be scandalized by him.

bibl.author: Valerius Maximus, Facta et dicta memorabilia Valerii Maximi

cit.quote: Valerius, on a certain young man of marvelous beauty, and this in book 4.
As Gregory says, the dove is a messenger of peace, and signifies peace.

It signifies the order of the Friars Minor, who preach peace, desire peace, and announce peace. Genesis 8: the dove — and this is the order of the Minorites — came to him, that is, to the ecclesiastical assembly, at evening, that is, around the world's old age, carrying an olive branch with green leaves in its mouth.
Ambrose, in the blessing-prayer for palms: 'God, who by the olive branch bid the dove announce that peace had been restored to the earth,' and so on.
A figure of simplicity: for it is a most simple animal, both in its look and in its regard, or gaze.
It signifies evangelical men, conducting themselves like the dove, without duplicity or malice. Matthew 10: 'be simple as doves.'
It is written of blessed Dominic that this made him most pleasing to all: that, walking a simple path, he never showed any trace of duplicity or pretense.
'That the merits of the saint may be rewarded in the newly-born, he hands on to them, in this new age, the way of simplicity.'
Clean birds, Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14.
It signifies the dove cherishing chastity, and keeping it from childhood. Song of Songs 6: 'my dove, my perfect one, is but one.'
It is written of blessed Martin that he was untouched by the vices to which that kind of man is usually entangled.
Blessed Augustine also writes, in the book of Confessions, that Ambrose's celibacy seemed to him a laborious thing.
Eighteenth, as the same author says, it is fruitful in offspring.
It signifies those abounding in many good works. Proverbs 15: 'in abundant justice, there is the greatest strength.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, De celesti hierarchia

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy: 'it is the property of virtue to progress always and continually.'
Nineteenth, as the same author says, it is a rival of piety; for it is a very fitting representation of piety, both in its look and in its groan.
It signifies religious and pious men, who display and pursue piety both in habit, and in look, and in effect. Ecclesiasticus 44: 'these are men of mercy, whose godly deeds have not failed.'
Blessed Ambrose said to Augustine's mother, who frequently and tearfully begged him for her son's conversion: 'go; for it is impossible that the son of so many tears should perish.'

Augustine also writes, in the book of Confessions, of blessed Ambrose, that he was a champion of piety. Likewise there he states of his own mother that she was strong in piety, and cared for nothing but God and divine things.
Twentieth, as Jerome says, it is so unmindful of injury that, even when its young are taken from it, it does not cease to nest in the same place, having forgotten whatever loss it suffered.

It signifies the friends of God who, following Christ's example, bear no rancor or hatred, but forget losses and injuries, insults and reproaches, according to the pattern of the wise man: 'remember not any injury done to you by your neighbor,' Ecclesiasticus 10.
'I beg you to forget the crime of your brothers, and the wickedness that they practiced against you.'

It is written in the Summa of Collations of a certain philosopher, and likewise of a certain emperor, that, though they retained everything else in wondrous memory, they consigned only injuries to oblivion.

The dove, as Ambrose says in the Hexameron, is trained in Egypt and in Syria to be a bearer of letters, and a go-between from one province to another. For it naturally loves the place and dwelling where it was first raised, and however far it is carried off to distant regions, it always returns to its own home, if it is set free. And to such a dove they are accustomed to bind a letter carefully under its wing, and, once released, it raises itself into the air, and never stops until it returns to the first places of its birth.

It signifies household servants, or officials, who are good, faithful, and useful, acting well and usefully and effectively and constantly handling and managing their master's goods, and recognizing his earlier kindnesses. Ecclesiasticus 7: 'let a wise servant be dear to you as your own soul; do not defraud him of his liberty, nor leave him needy.'
It is written in the legend of the blessed martyrs Vitalis and Agricola that good servitude and good liberty are weighed by God on an equal scale.
Twenty-second, as is known by experience, it has red, or ruddy, feet.
It signifies a man inflamed, in his affections, with divine love. Song of Songs 5: 'my beloved is white and ruddy.'
Blessed Agnes said, as is found in her passion: 'I have received honey and milk from his mouth, and his blood has adorned my cheeks.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Twenty-third, as Gregory puts it in the Moralia: 'it is foolishly curious.' For, sitting upon a tree, it looks around, and, as though deliberating, turns its neck this way and that, as to which side it wishes to settle. But often, while it deliberates over its flight, before it takes flight, an arrow flies past it, and so it does not complete its purpose, since what it proposed to do for so long, it fails to accomplish at the fitting time.

It signifies certain men wise in their own eyes, against the pattern of the Apostle in Romans 12, who, leaning on their own prudence, and setting no limit to their own wisdom, against the pattern given in Proverbs 3 and 23, while always proposing good things and not doing them, are overtaken by death or hell, and find themselves frustrated and deceived.
And this is what Hosea means, when he says in chapter 7: 'Ephraim has become like a deceived dove' — another reading has 'a dove forestalled' — 'without heart.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Epistola Hieronymi ad Paulinum presbyterum

cit.quote: Against which blessed Jerome says, to Paulinus the priest, who had a holy desire but was putting off the work: 'hasten, I beg you, and, for the little boat clinging to the swell, rather cut the rope than loosen it.' He easily despises all things who always thinks himself about to die.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Commentarii Hieronymi in prophetas minores

cit.quote: The dove is naturally timid, and rarely secure, except when it gathers itself into the cleft of the rock, where it rests, in some measure.

It signifies the fainthearted, who do not truly trust, but always exist, or remain, in faintheartedness and dread. Job 15: 'the sound of dread is always in his ears; and when there is peace, he suspects treachery. He believes not that he may return from darkness to light, looking round about every way for the sword.' Against which the wise man says: 'every land is a homeland to the brave,' and 'to the brave and great of soul, every day is one and the same.'

bibl.author: De dietis universalibus et particularibus Isaac Israeli

cit.quote: Twenty-fifth, as is said in the Diets, its flesh is hard and viscous to digest. Hence it gives coarse nourishment, especially the flesh of squabs before their first flight; and the older it is, the harder and worse it becomes.

It signifies those hardened in mind and steeped in youthful lust, and grown old, too, in their sins. Romans 2: 'but according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you treasure up to yourself wrath, against the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God.'
'Grown old in evil days,' and so on.
Isaiah 65: 'the child shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner being a hundred years old shall be accursed.'

Against which, it is read of blessed Martin that 'the holy childhood of this illustrious boy breathed rather of divine servitude'; and of blessed Jerome, that he took up the garment of Christ as a boy, at Rome.

Twenty-sixth, as the author says, a tame dove is sometimes found that is trained to deceive wild ones. For, joining itself to the wild doves, it leads them to the net, and, so as to deceive them more cautiously, it enters the fowler's net together with them, and lets itself be entangled under the guise of friendship, and, as though luring them to pasture, drags them into the snare and to their destruction.

It signifies vultures, and deceivers, and procurers or procuresses of debauchery, who, under the pretext of giving pleasure, lead men into the torments of hell, and entangle them in the snare of final punishment. Ecclesiastes 7: 'I have found a woman more bitter than death, who is the hunter's snare, and her heart a net, and her hands are bands. He that pleases God shall escape from her; but he that is a sinner shall be caught by her.'
Origen, in the homily On the Canaanite Woman: 'woman, the head of sin, the weapon of the devil, the expulsion from paradise, the corruption of the old law.'

Twenty-seventh, as the author says, it is trainable for performing deceptions, as is clear from the example of Muhammad's dove which, as is written in the accounts of his deeds, while it picked grains from his ear before the people, was believed to be delivering the divine law to Muhammad's ears by revelation.

It signifies young people who let themselves be seduced and drawn to every side. Proverbs 7: 'I see a foolish young man,' and immediately after it follows that he follows a harlot, 'as a lamb playing wantonly, and as an ox led to be a victim; and he knows not that a fool is being drawn to bonds, and that it concerns the danger of his soul.'

Against which, it is read of blessed Benedict, in book 2 of the Dialogues, that, 'surpassing his years in conduct, he gave his soul to no pleasure, fearing lest, if he touched anything of worldly knowledge, he too would go headlong into some terrible precipice.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Commentarii Hieronymi in prophetas minores

cit.quote: Twenty-eighth, as Jerome says on the minor prophets, the more feathered it is, the more fruitful it is found to be. Hence doves that have feathered feet breed almost every month.
It signifies men filled with virtues and gifts of grace, fruitful in the Church and in the household. James 3: 'the wisdom that is from above is full of mercy and good fruits.'
'In abundant justice, there is the greatest strength.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke, also read in a homily On Palm Sunday: 'for who else would bear such fruits of olive trees — not curved down by the fullness of their berries, but by the fullness of the spirit of the fruitful nations'? 'I,' he says, 'like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in his mercy,' and so on.
Quail are found to have these conditions, or properties.
For first, as Isidore says, they are birds having fixed times for coming, and forming and leading a flock.
They signify those living in regular order and in community. Psalm 132: 'behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, De paradiso Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Blessed Ambrose gives an example, in the book On Paradise, where he says that there were fifteen hundred servants of God at once in the desert, worshiping God together under father Pachomius.
Likewise, blessed Jerome, in letter 64, says that there were five hundred, in the desert of Egypt, serving God with a single diet and habit.
Second, as the same author says, they greatly fear the hawk; for as long as they see or sense it, they do not rise from the ground.

They signify that the devil is to be feared, and greatly guarded against, and watched for against his snares. 1 Peter 5: 'your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goes about, seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith.'

bibl.author: Leo Magnus, Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: Pope Leo, in a sermon On the Circumcision: 'the ancient enemy does not cease to spread the snares of deception everywhere, and to press on, so as to corrupt, by whatever means, the faith of believers.'

Third, as the same author says, these birds have leaders, as cranes do too, and, since they fear hawks, they are careful to consult their leaders, by whom they are wary of their own dangers, lest they be caught.

They signify good subjects, choosing good and diligent prelates for themselves, and assisting them in their office, lest they incur any danger to souls. Acts 20: 'take heed to yourselves, and to the whole flock, wherein the Holy Spirit has placed you bishops, to rule the Church which he has purchased with his own blood.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: Bernard, to Eugenius: let shepherds be such as to be 'upright in judgment, provident in counsel, discreet in commanding, diligent in disposing.'
Fourth, as the same [Isidore] says, this bird, crossing the sea, when it grows weary, descends into the water, and, raising one wing, makes for itself a sail.

It signifies that the just man, in his vexations, ought to take refuge in the tears of devotion, and expose his soul to heavenly influences, or gifts of grace. Psalm 76: 'in the day of my trouble I sought God, with my hands lifted up to him in the night, and I was not deceived.'
...marvelously overcame the demons sent by the philosophers, four in number, since he was always found praying, or reading divine things, weeping, or signing himself with the cross.
Fifth, as the same author puts it, these birds are most pleasing for food.

They signify the consolations of heavenly grace, or the refreshments of the venerable Scripture. Wisdom 16: 'you have well disposed of your people, preparing for them a new taste, the quail.' The same bird has two names.

bibl.author: Iohannes Damascenus, De fide orthodoxa Iohannis Damasceni

cit.quote: Damascene, in his little book: 'let us knock at the paradise of the sacred Scriptures, which is best, which, god-bearing, flies about our ears.'
Sixth, as blessed Ambrose puts it, they greatly love their own kind, and so call to one another with their cries.
They signify a common charity within a household, or congregation, and a mutual encouragement to good. 1 Peter 4: 'but before all things, having a mutual and continual charity among yourselves.'
'Exhort one another, day by day.'
Blessed Francis says in his Rule: 'wherever the brothers may be, and find one another, let them show themselves to be members of the same household,' and so on.
Seventh, as Isidore says, they run most swiftly over the ground.
They signify strong progress in good, Psalm 83: 'they shall go from strength to strength,' and so on.

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, De celesti hierarchia

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy: 'it is the property of virtue always and continually to progress.'
'The sparrow, a bird.'

It signifies the greedy, or those falling by habit into sin. 1 Timothy, last chapter, 9: 'they that will become rich fall into temptation, and into the snare of the devil, and into many hurtful desires, which drown men in destruction and perdition.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Epistola Hieronymi ad Paulinum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, to Paulinus: 'even an obol is wanting to the unbeliever.'
Ninth, as the same author says, they have poisonous seeds, for their food is hellebore, on account of which the ancients forbade eating them.
Hence, if it is taken from the animal in great quantity, it will harm the one who consumes it. They signify that the consolations of this world are poisoned.

For their food and refreshment are suspect both in their beginning and their end, and so, if they are taken through habit, or excess, they harm the soul. 1 John 2: 'love not the world, nor the things that are in the world; for all that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, and the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life.'
The Gloss, on chapter 1 of blessed James's letter: 'the wicked have nothing in heaven, and you have nothing in the world.'
Tenth, as the same author says, they have veins around the heart, and so they digest hellebore.

They signify, according to Proverbs, that those who have a strict conscience, rather than a loose one, are able the more, and the better, to remove themselves from sins and vices, and to rise above the various desires of this world: 'blessed is the man who is always fearful; but he that is hardened in mind shall fall into evil.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia, and elsewhere: 'it is the mark of good minds to recognize guilt where there is no guilt.'
The stork is found, according to the authorities, to have these conditions, or properties.

For first, as Isidore says, it is a river-bird, purging itself with its own beak. For when, from the abundance of food, it feels itself weighed down, it draws seawater up into its neck, and pours it, through its rear passage, into its inner parts, which, by softening the hardness of the packed food and cleansing the intestines, it casts out and expels the excess.

It signifies the purging of a soul filled with sins, or poisonous vices, through contrition and confession. Psalm 31: 'I said: I will confess against myself my injustices to the Lord, and you have forgiven the wickedness of my sin.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia, and elsewhere: 'a sin that is not quickly washed away through penance soon drags, by its own weight, toward another.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, this bird feeds on serpents' eggs, and brings the most pleasing food from them to its young.

It signifies that detractors feed on, and feed others with, the infamies and venomous bites of others. Proverbs 30: 'a generation that has swords for teeth, and grinds with its jaw-teeth, to devour the needy from off the earth, and the poor from among men.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'he strikes charity in all who hear him, with his cursed tongue, and thoroughly kills and extinguishes it.'
Against which, James 3: 'detract not one from another,' and so on.
Third, as the same Isidore says, the stork ('ciconia') is called, as it were, 'cicannia,' since it makes a sound, as with a reed, by clattering its beak.
It signifies the talkative, or garrulous. Proverbs 10: 'in much talk there shall not want sin.'
'Have you seen a man hasty to speak? Folly is rather to be hoped for than his amendment.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, De celesti hierarchia

cit.quote: Against which, Dionysius, On the Angelic Hierarchy, near the end: 'with due silence, we preserve God's secret within ourselves.'
Fourth, as the same Isidore says, it is the messenger of spring, and, in its coming, proclaims the newness of the season.
It signifies the preachers of the Gospel, preaching and announcing eternal life. 1 John 1: 'we bear witness, and declare to you, eternal life, which was with the Father, and has appeared to us.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily for the Second Sunday of Pentecost: 'a certain man made a great supper, and invited many,' since the eternal God has prepared an eternal refreshment, and does not cease inviting men of every nation and age to it, through preachers.
Fifth, as the same Isidore says, it is an enemy to serpents: for it strikes and kills them with its beak, and sometimes devours and swallows them whole.

It signifies the hatred between demons and evil men. Ecclesiasticus 13: 'what fellowship shall the earthen pot have with the kettle? For when they shall knock one against the other, it shall be broken.'
Ambrose, in a sermon On the Lord's Passion: 'so does the devil love the sinner, as a glutton loves a fattened bird, so as to eat it.' Such is the devil's love for his own.
As the same Isidore says, it loves company and frequent companionship, and so it is accustomed to nest on the roofs of houses inhabited by men.
It signifies those who follow and love the assembly, or congregation. Ecclesiasticus 4: 'be affable to the congregation of the poor.'
Psalm 132: 'behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.'

Blessed Jerome gives an example, in the Lives of the Fathers, of the elder hermits who gathered together every Sunday for Mass and an exhortation for their edification, and sometimes for the refreshment of the body.

It does not easily give up its first nest, unless forced; but, in withdrawing for winter, it fills it with earth, and binds together the twigs and thorns of the nest with mud, lest some stormy wind cast it down or destroy it in winter. But on its return in spring it takes back or occupies the same place, and protects and defends it against others wishing to occupy the nest.

It signifies that everyone ought to be content with his own calling, and ought to be diligent and solicitous in preserving it. 1 Corinthians 7: 'let every man walk as God has called him. Let every man abide in the same calling in which he was called, before God.'

Blessed Jerome relates, in the Lives of the Fathers, of John the simple hermit, who, not being content with the common life, cast off the cloak of company and went into a more remote desert, wishing to live free and secure in the manner of the angels, not of men. But when a week had passed, he returned, since he could not keep his resolve, and the door was not opened to him — indeed, he was reproached, that John had become an angel. And so, rebuked, he returned to his beginnings, and lived thereafter as the others did.

The female — the male does not join with another for the purpose of coupling, but keeps faith with the female as regards the nest and the office of raising the young. In her, if the male by some chance suspects an adulterous coupling, he no longer dwells with her, but strikes her through with his beak, if he can, and kills her; nor does he ever mount another female except in the nest.

It signifies the fidelity of marriage, and its zeal and honesty. 1 Thessalonians 4: 'let every one of you know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, as the Gentiles that know not God. For God has not called us unto uncleanness,' and so on.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'the virginity of holy Mary, betrothed to Joseph, is thus preserved — inviolable in reputation, just as it is whole in modesty. Nor was it fitting that, for virgins living under sinister opinion, an excuse for a veil should be left, by which the mother of the Lord too might seem to be defamed.'

Ninth, as the same author says, and blessed Ambrose likewise: the male and female take turns brooding on the eggs; the father loves and guards his young with affection, and, from his constant sitting upon them, loses his feathers. Also, when he is out at pasture, the mother stays on the nest; and, conversely, when the male returns, the female flies off to pasture, and the male tends the nest.
