It signifies that, from evil examples, or destructive works, evil men arise and are cherished and nourished in vices. Exodus 5: 'you have made our savor to stink before Pharaoh and his servants.'
Hence it is said that many are corrupted by the evil example of one man.

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus, De copia verborum

cit.quote: Seneca, On the Four Virtues: 'many affirm the king's lie.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, De heresibus Augustini ad Quodvultdeum

cit.quote: Augustine, Against Arius: 'the punishment of Arius is not fixed, since it is not yet known how many will be ruined by his evil example.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Epistola Hieronymi ad Letam de institutione filie

cit.quote: 'It is easy to be a rival of evils, and you quickly imitate the vices of those whose virtues you cannot attain.' Greek history relates that Alexander, the most powerful of kings, and lord of the world, could not, in his character and his very gait, be free of the vices of Leonidas, his tutor, with which he had been infected while still a small boy. Thus far Jerome.
The diving-bird is found to have these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities.

For first, as Isidore says, it took its name from its constant diving; for often, plunging its head into the deep, it gathers the signs of the winds beneath the waves, and, before a violent storm at sea, makes for the shore with a cry.
For it is most certain that there will be a very heavy storm at sea when diving-birds flee to the shore with a cry, as the same Isidore says.

It signifies greedy rich men, or the merchants of this world, who, for the gains of this world, plunge themselves into vices and sins, their minds turned away from God, and do not return to God except when they are overtaken or seized by the very heaviest storms of sickness, according to that saying, Psalm 15: 'their infirmities were multiplied; afterward they made haste.'

'For the desire of money is the root of all evils; which some coveting have erred from the faith. For they that will become rich fall into temptation, and into the snare of the devil, and into many unprofitable and hurtful desires, which drown men in destruction and perdition.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Epistola Hieronymi ad Paulinum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, in the letter to Paulinus: 'to the believer the whole world is a treasury of riches; but the unbeliever lacks even a single coin.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, the diving-bird nests among reeds, upon few sticks of wood.

bibl.author: Apostolus, Epistola Pauli ad Timotheum prima

cit.quote: It signifies religious content with their own poverty, after the pattern of the Apostle, 1 Timothy, the last chapter: 'and having food, and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content.'

Peter, in the Itinerary, speaking to Clement: 'bread with olives, and rarely also with vegetables, is my usual food. As for the clothing you see, a tunic with a cloak, with these I am content, and require no more,' and so on.

Third, as the same Isidore says, by a certain wondrous natural affection it nourishes and raises its chicks; who, as soon as they are born, follow their father, and are not afraid to ascend or descend the various waves of the sea.

They signify good prelates, affectionately forming and cherishing their subjects; and likewise good subjects, obediently following their prelates out of affection, in prosperity and adversity alike: 'for what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you, before our Lord Jesus Christ? For you are our glory and our joy.'
'In three things my spirit is delighted, which are approved before God and men: the concord of brethren, the love of neighbors, and man and wife well agreeing together.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, De paradiso Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Many examples are given by blessed Jerome, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, and by Cassian, in the Conferences of the Fathers, of how, in the desert of Egypt, abbots lived together with their disciples: the fathers instructing them in spiritual things, the disciples obeying every command. Likewise, blessed Ambrose says, in the book On Paradise, that, under father Pachomius, fifteen hundred served God in perfect charity.
Fourth, as the same Isidore says, it hunts water-worms and little fish, to feed its own gluttony.

They signify the powerful of this age, who oppress the poor and their inferiors, to feed their avarice and greed. James 2: 'do not the rich oppress you by might? And do not they draw you before the judgment seats? Do not they blaspheme, by their deeds, the good name that is invoked upon you?'

An example is found in two famous and powerful philosophers who came to tempt blessed Anthony, the poor monk, as Jerome relates in the Lives of the Fathers, and strove to disturb and oppress him not only in person, but also through magic arts, or demonic dealings; but divine power protected its servant, and rescued him from their violence and effort.
Fifth, as the same Isidore says, in winter, because of the scarcity of their movement, birds grow fat; but in summer, because of the freedom of their flight, they are impoverished of flesh and fat.

They signify, as to the first, the rich of this world, dissolved in their ease and delights; as to the second, the religious of the Gospel, poor in all things and deprived of carnal consolations. Luke 6: 'woe to you rich, who have here your consolation'; there too: 'blessed are the poor, for theirs is the kingdom of God.' An example is found in the rich feaster and the beggar Lazarus.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, De officiis ministrorum Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Ambrose, in the book On the Duties of Ministers: 'riches provide no help toward a blessed life. This the Lord clearly showed in the Gospel, when he said: "blessed are the poor," and "woe to you rich."'
As the same Isidore says, when diving-birds are attacked by a bird of prey, they take refuge in the water, and are freed by the benefit of diving under.

They signify those who, wishing to flee the snares of the devil, or the world, or the flesh, or of any sin or vice, or of adversity, hasten to religion, in which there is the pool of penance, where they wash themselves and are freed from dangers. Isaiah 32: 'and a man shall be as when one is hidden from the wind, and hides himself from a storm, as rivers of waters in a time of drought, and as the shadow of a rock that stands out in a desert land.'
'Behold, I have gone far off flying, and I remained in the wilderness. I waited for him that has saved me from pusillanimity of spirit, and a storm.'

Bernard, in a certain sermon that begins 'we shall go a three days' journey,' and so on: 'what security, what benefit, does solitude bring? John the Baptist clearly showed it, who, seeing the wickedness and contention in the city, preferred solitude to the city, and the monastic life to the priesthood, knowing no dangers or death for as long as he dwelt in the desert. What virtue, what gain for the mind, he won there, is clear. For he became such a man in solitude that he alone washed Christ, who washes all things, and, for the sake of truth, shrank from neither death nor prison.' Thus far Bernard.
Blessed Ambrose writes, of the diving-bird, in the Hexameron, book 5, chapters 17 and 26, that its song is most sweet and wondrous.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: It signifies the angelic harmony, of which, mystically, Job 38 speaks, and Gregory, in the same passage.
The kite is found to have these conditions, or properties.

For first, as Isidore says, the kite is soft in flight and in strength; hence the kite ('miluus') is named as it were flying softly ('molliter uolans'). For it is borne through the air on a light and, as it were, motionless wing, and, in flying, seems scarcely to stir the air even with a light touch.

It signifies flatterers, or even traitors, carrying out their vices softly, or smoothly, and cautiously, and step by step. Hosea 12: 'Ephraim feeds on wind, and follows the burning heat; all the day long he multiplies lying and desolation; he made a covenant with the Assyrians, and carried oil into Egypt.'
Augustine, in a homily, or rather a sermon, on the parable of the Ten Virgins: 'all flatterers sell oil.'
'Let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: 'By the name of oil, flattery is unhesitatingly understood.'

Second, as the same Isidore says, it is a bird patient of labor, and so it takes cuckoos onto its shoulders, and, lest they fail from weariness over the long distances of the journey, carries them with it from the regions of Spain.
It signifies certain men favoring and showing partiality toward base and unworthy persons who hold the place of cuckoos in the Church.

Or, better, if we wish, it signifies those who, from the strength of their body, or the ease granted them, supply others from the depths of their piety, or works of charity, following the pattern of the Apostle Peter, 1 Peter 4: 'as every man has received grace, administering the same to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.'

Blessed Jerome gives an example, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, of a certain father to whom a special grace was given from heaven, since, devoting himself to works of piety, when he was once among robbers, he snatched a certain virgin from their hands, and led back another, corrupted, who had gone astray.
...a bird of prey, bold with the smallest, but timid with the great. For it does not dare to attack wild birds, but does not fear to lie in wait for domestic ones.

It signifies certain prelates, or mercenary zealots, that is, those existing in the Church for the sake of temporal reward, who devote care and zeal, as though fervent, to correcting the smallest failings in lesser brothers, or subjects, but do not dare, or neglect, to correct or reprove greater sins, or vices, in those greater than themselves. Matthew 23: 'woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint, and rue, and cumin, and every herb, and leave undone the weightier things of the law, and pass over judgment and the love of God.'

Blessed Jerome gives an example, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, of a certain brother in whose face divine grace clearly shone forth, or rather, gleamed openly, who lost this brightness because, being a Pharisee, he judged a certain brother of his eating on Friday morning. For what he ought to have attributed to necessity, out of charity, he attributed instead to gluttony, or greed, out of a recklessness arising from presumption in his own righteousness.

And while he took care over small things, he fell into serious, or great, ones, according to that saying, Ecclesiasticus 19: 'he that despises small things shall fall by little and little,' according to another reading.
Augustine, On the Words of the Gospel: 'if your brother, complaining of his stomach, says that he cannot fast, and you attribute this to the vice of gluttony, you have judged rashly.'
Fourth, as the same Isidore says, it lies in wait marvelously for chicks, to seize them, and, whichever it finds unguarded, kills at once.

It signifies demons lying in wait for those newly converted in the faith, or the powerful of this age lying in wait for their poor vassals, or other humble and simple folk, to extort their goods or profits. Proverbs 28: 'a leader void of prudence shall oppress many by his power. As a roaring lion, and a hungry bear, so is a wicked ruler over the poor people.'

bibl.author: Passio sanctorum Gallicani Iohannis et Pauli

cit.quote: An example is found in Julian the Apostate, who, coloring his own greed with the testimony of the Gospel, said to blessed John and Paul, as is found in their passion, whose goods he thirsted for: 'our Christ says in the Gospel: he that does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.'

...the emperor Decius who, as is found in the passion of blessed Lawrence, sought so eagerly and diligently for the treasures of the Church, which had already been distributed to the poor by blessed Lawrence, and had them sought after.

Fifth, as the same Isidore says, it feeds on carcasses and unclean things, and, for the sake of a small feeding of its belly, stoops to attack whatever flesh it can, even the most vile, and is greedily carried about.

It signifies the gluttonous, given over to every food, and solicitous for every carnal food, whereas they ought to be more eager and solicitous for the nourishment of the soul, which is better. Ecclesiasticus 36: 'the belly will eat every food, but one food is better than another.'
'Food for the belly, and the belly for food; but God shall destroy both it and them.'
Against which, Ecclesiasticus 31: 'use, like a frugal man, what is set before you, lest, when you eat much, you be hated.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: For it is not necessary to praise frugality in him, since he used it at that time in such a way that he was thought not so much a soldier as a monk.
Augustine, in the Confessions: 'you have commanded, Lord, that I should approach food as I would medicine.'
Sixth, as the same Isidore says, it is attacked by the sparrowhawk, and, because of its own faintheartedness and sluggishness, is overcome by a bird smaller than itself.

It signifies those who are timid in attacking difficult things, and lazy in doing praiseworthy ones, and less than manly in overcoming temptations posed by a weak enemy. Proverbs 26: 'the slothful man says, "there is a lion in the way, and a lioness in the roads." I shall be killed in the midst of the streets.' The sluggard hides his hands under his armpits, and so on.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia, and elsewhere: 'the enemy is weak, who cannot conquer one who is unwilling.'
In its youth, the kite does not seem to differ from other birds of prey, but the longer it lives, the more it shows a degenerate nature.

It signifies those who, at the beginning of their conversion, or advancement, in religion or in the Church, are devout, but, as time goes on, degenerate and grow lukewarm. Galatians 3: 'are you so foolish, that, whereas you began in the spirit, you would now be made perfect by the flesh?'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, De celesti hierarchia

cit.quote: Against which, Dionysius, in the book On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy: 'it is the property of virtue to progress continually and always.'

As Aristotle says, there is a certain kind of kite that, at first, seizes birds, then, afterward, eats such small animals, and finally scarcely catches flies and little worms, and, at the last, dies of hunger.

It signifies those who, being noble by nature, presume greatly in their youth, but, as age advances, and in old age itself, fail utterly, both spiritually and temporally. Jeremiah 15: 'her light is gone down, while it was yet day.'
1 Kings 2: 'she that had seven sons is weakened.'

Against such men, blessed Bernard says: 'many know many things, and do not know themselves. They look at others, and abandon themselves. They seek God through these outward things, abandoning their own inward parts, in which the inward God dwells.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: 'He to whom God is his portion ought to care for nothing but God.'

Ninth, as the author says, it is unkind toward its own young, like the vulture. For it grieves when it sees them growing fat, and, so that they may waste away, strikes them with its beak, and withholds their food.
It signifies evil prelates, or teachers, who envy the advancement of their subjects, or disciples. Job 39: 'she is hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers.'
Against which, Galatians 4: 'my little children, of whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs, to shepherds: 'bring forth the breasts, suspend the blows.'
Tenth, as the same Isidore says, it has a plaintive voice, a messenger of hunger; for when it is hungry, it seeks food with a plaintive cry.

It signifies preachers concerned with gain, who, consulting their own greed, always plead to the world their lack of necessary things. 1 Timothy, last chapter: 'the wranglings of men corrupted in mind, and who are destitute of the truth, supposing gain to be godliness.'
Micah 3: 'if any man gives not something for their mouths, they prepare war against him.'
...of Julian the Apostate, and the emperor Decius, who raged and strove to extort treasures, as is found in the Historia Tripartita.
The night-raven, which blessed Ambrose also calls the night-owl, in the Hexameron, is found to have these properties, or conditions.
The night-raven ('nycticorax') is so called, as it were, the raven of night, since it loves the night. For, flying by night, it seeks food, and, seeking it, cries out.

It signifies those who walk in pretense, and not in the light, and yet, in a spirit or appearance of piety, seek their living by begging. 2 Timothy 3: 'having an appearance of godliness, but denying its power.'
An example is found in the poor men of Lyon, and other heretics, described in the last question of the twenty-sixth Cause, and in the Decretals, Extra, On Heretics: 'We excommunicate.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, its cry is hateful to other birds.

It signifies the voice of preaching, or of prayer, hateful to demons and their like. 3 John: 'I would have written, perhaps, to the church: but Diotrephes, who loves to have the pre-eminence among them, does not receive us. For this cause, if I come, I will admonish his deeds which he does, prating against us with malicious words.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'do you wish to know the gifts of God? The garments of Paul were a terror to demons.' The same: 'the wicked cannot bear to see what is good.'
Third, as the same Isidore says, it is a bird that flees the light, and cannot bear to see the sun.
It signifies those whose deeds are in darkness, fleeing the light of truth. John 3: 'every one that does evil hates the light, and comes not to the light, that his works may not be reproved.'
'For the things that are done by them in secret, it is shameful even to speak of.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, De ecclesiastica hierarchia Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy: 'the manner of withdrawing from the light is twofold, namely either through malice, or by going beyond measure, or by following desire.'
Fourth, as the same Isidore puts it, it inhabits and frequents tombs and the places of the dead.
It signifies the devil dwelling in souls deprived of Christ, of life, and of charity: 'and Satan entered into Judas, who was surnamed Iscariot,' and so on.
The Gloss, on Mark: 'the devil had entered where Christ had gone out.'
Fifth, as the same Isidore says, it nests in walls and in cracked places.

It signifies that the devil especially helps himself, through hypocrites and heretics, toward the multiplication of his members, or his children. 2 Timothy 3: 'for of these sort are they who creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins, who are led away with divers desires.'
Pope Leo: 'the ancient enemy has very many whom he has bound to himself so tightly that he makes use of their wits and their tongues for the deception of others.'
It breaks and devours the eggs of doves and of jackdaws, and fights with them.

It signifies corrupt men corrupting the simple members of the Church, still tender in faith, and ready in holy will for good works. 1 Corinthians 15: 'be not seduced: evil communications corrupt good manners.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, De heresibus Augustini ad Quodvultdeum

cit.quote: Augustine, On Heretics: 'the punishment of Arius is not fixed, since it is not known how many will perish through his evil example, or teaching.'
'Many seducers have gone out into the world, who confess not that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.'
The night-owl ('noctua'), as it were seeing by night ('de nocte tuens'), since it sees keenly by night; but when the brightness of the sun rises, its sight is dulled.

It signifies, according to blessed Ambrose in the Hexameron, where he treats of the night-owl, the wise of this world, blind to divine things, but sharp and keen-sighted for worldly ones. Jeremiah 4: 'they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge.'

Jerome, in the letter On the Twelve Luminaries: 'Heliodorus the priest, looking into a house through a small opening, and, indeed, testing the door, but having no key, remained empty within, his eyes open outside.'
Eighth, as the same Isidore says, the island of Crete does not have this bird, and if it should come from elsewhere, it will die at once.
It signifies that religion does not endure the wicked, from wherever they may come to it. Apocalypse 2: 'but this you have, that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus, Epistole Senece ad Lucilium

cit.quote: Seneca, to Lucilius: 'the first step of innocence is to hate wicked things.'

'I know your works, and your patience and labor, and that you cannot bear the wicked, and you have tried them who say they are apostles and are not, and have found them liars, and you have not fainted.'
The onocrotalus is found, according to the ancients, to have these properties, or conditions.
For first, as Isidore says, it is a bird that makes a sound in the water.

It signifies those who boast in the pomp, or desire, of this world; against which, 1 Corinthians 9: 'I therefore so run, not as at an uncertainty; I so fight, not as one beating the air; but I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot know divine things.'

Second, as the same Isidore says, it is a very gluttonous bird, and has, in its throat, certain pouches, in which it first receives its food, and then sends what it has received into its second stomach, since it is a very gluttonous bird. For it has two stomachs: in one it receives only food, in the other it only cooks and digests it; but the first is reckoned as a pouch of the throat.

It signifies the gluttonous and the voracious, who care more for their belly than for virtue, intent, in body and soul, only on carnal pleasure. Romans, last chapter: 'for such men do not serve the Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly, and, by sweet words and blessings, seduce the hearts of the innocent.'

'The Lord called for weeping, and for mourning, for baldness, and for girding with sackcircle; and behold, joy and gladness, killing calves, and slaying rams. Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs, in his sermons: 'the pleasure of gluttony, so highly esteemed today, occupies scarcely the breadth of two fingers.'
Third, as the same Isidore says, it especially lies in wait for eels, and, swallowing the prey it has caught whole and at once, sends it down into its belly.

It signifies demons, and the cursed, and detractors, especially lying in wait for those who flee the world, since they find in them nothing by which to be terrified. 2 Timothy 3: 'know also this, that, in the last days, shall come dangerous times,' and so on: 'men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'A cursed tongue strikes charity in all, and, as far as lies in it, thoroughly kills and extinguishes it.'

As the same Isidore puts it, resting on the shore, it always keeps its beak raised upward, and so, by its sharpness, guards itself beforehand against the attack of the hawk, so that it may sleep more safely.

It signifies those who oppose their prelates, so as to remain, or grow numb, more safely in their sin or vice. 2 Timothy 3: 'now as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupted.'

An example is found in Elymas the sorcerer, and in Simon Magus, and in Julian the Apostate, and in many others, of whom Acts 13 and afterward speak, and the Historia Tripartita, and the Ecclesiastical History.
The pelican is found to have these conditions, or properties, according to the doctors.
For first, as Isidore says, it is 'an Egyptian bird dwelling in the wilderness beside the Nile.'

It signifies preachers and contemplatives fleeing worldly vanities and dwelling upon heavenly consolations, or the pleasant considerations and refreshments of the holy Scriptures, Psalm 54: 'lo, I have gone far off, and fled away, and I abode in the wilderness. I waited for him that has saved me from pusillanimity of spirit, and a storm.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'Divine consolation is a delicate thing, and is not given to those who possess what belongs to another.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot know divine things.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, whatever it eats it first dips in the water with its foot, and, once dipped as though with a hand, it applies and brings its foot to its mouth.
It signifies doctors, or preachers, who do what they teach, or preach, after the example of the apostle, Romans 15: 'for I dare not speak of any of those things which Christ works not by me.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: 'Let not your deeds put your words to shame, lest, when you speak in church, someone silently say: physician, heal yourself.'
As the same Isidore says, the pelican alone among birds, besides the phylargus, uses its foot in place of a hand.

It signifies the devout religious who, very often and for the most part, out of holy affection and desire, employs sacred meditations in place of manual occupation, 1 Timothy 4: 'exercise yourself unto godliness. For bodily exercise is profitable to little; but godliness is profitable to all things,' and so on.
It is written of blessed Martin that his eyes and hands were always intent upon heaven, and he never relaxed his unconquered spirit from prayer.

As Isidore says, the pelican is an excessive lover of its own young. For when it begets young and they begin to grow, they strike their parents in the face, on account of which the mother strikes them back and kills them, and mourns them for two days; but on the third day the mother strikes herself in the side, even to the shedding of blood, and pours the warm blood over the bodies of her dead young, by whose power the dead chicks come back to life.

It signifies the excessive love Christ had for the human race created by him, to be redeemed from death by the sprinkling of his blood on the cross and by his resurrection on the third day: 'who loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood.'
Revelation 5: 'you have redeemed us, Lord God, in your blood.'

Anselm, in the second book of Why God Became Man: 'the passion of Christ availed for the redemption of a thousand thousand worlds, were there so many creatures, and it outweighs every number and magnitude of sins done and to be done.'

bibl.author: Iacobus de Vitriaco, Historia orientalis Iacobi de Vitriaco

cit.quote: Master James of Vitry, in his History of the East, gives another reason for the death of the pelican's chicks; for he says that while the mother leaves the nest for food, a serpent, creeping up the tree, stings and poisons her chicks, and, the mother returning to them, she is said to mourn for three days. Then, wounding herself in the breast, she sprinkles her blood over them, and so raises them from death.

It signifies the same thing said above, with the addition that the human race, killed and slain by the procurement and poisonous temptation of the ancient serpent, the devil, the Son of God, in the manner of a loving mother dying and warming with him, brought back to life with his own blood, Psalm 101: 'I am become like a pelican of the wilderness; I am like a night-raven in the house,' upon which the Gloss makes this very point.
Fifth, as the same Isidore says, it is a bird of great wings.

It signifies, in the contemplative man, the broad expanses of supernal desires, or supermental affections, which is signified in Ezekiel 17: 'a great eagle, with great wings, long-limbed, full of feathers, and of variety, came to Libanus, and took away the marrow of the cedar. The eagle, or pelican, is the man raised up to God, who is called great in virtue; of great wings, by reason of the dilation of his inward parts; full of feathers and of variety, by reason of the manifold gifts and graces and sacred habits; such a one goes to Libanus, which is interpreted as whitening, since he comes to the beauty of angelic chastity; and at last he takes away the marrow of the cedar, since he perceives the inmost sweetness of God most high, or of Christ, God and man, exalted above the choirs of angels.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, De celesti hierarchia

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Celestial Hierarchy: 'the Lord Jesus alone is sweet-smelling and fills the heart with delight.'

As the same Isidore says, it is of the greatest leanness, since whatever it swallows it soon emits again through excretion; for it has a slippery intestine, and so does not hold its food until it is fully absorbed.

It signifies those who macerate their flesh in imitation of the crucified Christ, and manfully and quickly cast off and remove from themselves, without any pleasure or consent, whatever delightful thing the world offers. Galatians 5: 'and they that are Christ's have crucified their flesh, with the vices and concupiscences.'

An example is found in blessed Eugenia, who, believed to be a man by Melania, a most wealthy citizen, when great riches were offered her, so that she would consent to unite with her, answered: 'let those like you keep your wealth; it delights us to beg with Christ.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Passio sancte Agnetis martyris Rome

cit.quote: Blessed Agnes answered likewise the prefect's son, who assailed her and offered her all the glory of the world, as Ambrose relates in her passion.
'The serpent.'
It signifies that religious and holy men are hated by the devil, especially by Satan. 2 Corinthians 2: 'let us not be deceived by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his devices.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: An example is found in blessed Martin, to whom, as is found in his Life, the devil said that he would oppose him wherever he went. And he answered: 'the Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.'

An example is also found in blessed Benedict, to whom, as Gregory relates, in book 2 of the Dialogues, the devil gave a temptation of the vice of lust, under the appearance of a blackbird — over which, nonetheless, that servant of the Most High God gained the triumph.

As the same Isidore says: when the mother, weakened by the great outpouring of blood by which she revives her children, the chicks thus revived come forth for food and, by natural affection, feed their weakened mother; the mother, gladly noticing this, once her strength is regained, cherishes and loves the children who feed her.
It signifies men grateful to God and to his kindnesses, or to mother Church and her spiritual nourishments. Colossians 3: 'let the peace of Christ rejoice in your hearts, and be grateful.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Morlanensis, De contemptu mundi Bernardi Morlanensis

cit.quote: 'Ingratitude and forgetfulness of God's kindnesses dries up the fountain of divine piety.'

Ninth, as the same Isidore says, the pelican sometimes has certain degenerate offspring who, knowing that their mother is weakened by the shedding of blood to revive them, take no care of her at all; the mother, noticing this, once her strength has returned, casts them off, and does not allow them to remain with her at all.

It signifies that God and the Church punish the ungrateful, and drive them from their grace. Hosea 4: 'because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you, that you shall not do the office of priesthood to me.'
An example is found in Lucifer, Adam, Saul, Manasseh, Uzziah, Haman, Antiochus, and so on, each of whom was rejected and cast down for his own ingratitude and pride.
The partridge is found, according to the doctors, to have these conditions, or properties.
For first, as Isidore says: 'it is an unclean bird; for the male mounts the male, and headlong lust forgets its sex.'

It signifies sinners acting against nature in works of the flesh. Romans 1: 'and, in like manner, the men also, leaving the natural use of the woman, have burned in their lust toward one another, men with men working that which is shameful, and receiving in themselves the recompense which was due to their error.'
'Demons blush to be present.'
And then, out of shame, they flee, according to what blessed Augustine himself says, that, because of the horror of this sin, the Son of God almost refrained from becoming incarnate.

Second, as the same Isidore says, and likewise Ambrose in the Hexameron, it is so deceitful that, snatching away eggs not its own, it broods over the eggs it has stolen. But this deceit brings no profit, since, once the chicks have heard the voice of their true mother, by a certain natural affection, they abandon the supposed mother who reared them, and return to her who bore them.
It signifies robbers and usurers, who, in the end, find themselves deceived. Ecclesiasticus 30: 'the rich man has labored in gathering substance, and, in the end, he becomes poor.'

Augustine, in the sermon On the Innocents: 'where there is gain, there is also loss. Gain in the chest, loss in the conscience. He took away the garment, and lost his faith. No one has unjust gain without just loss.'
Partridges do not labor at brooding over their eggs, as other birds do.

They signify the children of the powerful, of worldly men, and of usurers, leading a life of delights without labor. Job 21: 'their seed continues before them, a multitude of children, and of children's children, in their sight; their infants exult with their toys; they hold the timbrel and the harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ.'
Against which, Jerome relates, of the fathers of Egypt, in the Lives of the Fathers, that they led a very sober life from the labor of their own hands.
Fourth, as the same author puts it, it is a bird of marvelous cunning; for the mother flies about the hunter in circles until her chicks flee, and, once her chicks have fled, she herself flees too.
It signifies the care, diligence, and skill that fleshly parents have for their fleshly children, and for themselves, in a carnal way.

Against which, Ecclesiastes 2: 'again I hated all my industry, wherewith I had earnestly labored under the sun, being like to have an heir after me, whom I know not whether he shall be a wise man or a fool, and he shall have rule over all my labors, with which I have toiled, and been solicitous.'

Blessed Gregory gives an example, in book 4 of the Dialogues, of a certain man who, thinking he would live long — for the devil had deluded him thus in a dream — gathered all the goods he could, to enjoy with his own; and behold, the following night, suddenly and unexpectedly, he died, and was deprived of his hope.
Fifth, as the same author says, the mother is followed by her chicks, who, as soon as they are born, follow her and seek food.

It signifies that evil fathers instruct their children badly, and evil children become imitators of their fathers' crimes, and seekers of others' goods. Ecclesiasticus 41: 'unhappy are the children of sinners, they that keep company with the dwellings of the wicked. The inheritance of the children of sinners shall perish, and with their seed shall be a perpetual reproach. Wicked children shall complain of an impious father, because for his sake they are in reproach.'
'God, at Rome.'
...a bird of much flesh, especially in the breast, and of little feathering; and so its flight is weak, and, in flying, it raises itself little above the ground, but soon makes for the ground again.
It signifies those who are more carnal than spiritual, and so cling more to temporal things than to heavenly ones, and are more disposed toward earthly things than toward eternal ones.
For this reason they must cry out that prophetic saying: 'our belly has cleaved to the earth; arise, Lord, help us, and deliver us.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot know divine things.' Psalm 68: 'I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep,' and so on.
It fears and flees the sparrowhawk, and, as long as it sees it in the air, does not leave the ground.
It signifies base men, having a worldly and servile fear, not a divine one; against which, 1 John 4: 'fear is not in charity, but perfect charity casts out fear.'
Nothing at all was to be feared by Paul, except offending God. 'For he reckoned tyrants, and those breathing forth fury, to be, as it were, mere gnats.'
Eighth, as the same author says, fleeing at the sound of a little bell over the ground, before it knows it, it throws itself into a net or a snare.

It signifies those who flee the hearing of the divine office, or word, out of love for earthly things and preoccupation with them, and, in the end, fall into the snare of hell, when they do not turn away. Luke 8: 'going, they are choked with the cares, and riches, and pleasures of life, and yield no fruit.'
'He that turns away his ear from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination.'
It is asked: why did Aegisthus become an adulterer? The cause is at hand: he was idle.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Ninth, as Pliny says, in book 29, chapter 6: 'the gall of partridges, mixed with an equal weight of honey, greatly clarifies the sight; hence it ought to be kept in a silver box.'

It signifies that the bitterness of Christ's passion, and of the martyrs, and its deep and devout consideration, greatly clarifies the sight of the mind and cleanses the affections — which is indeed proven to be always kept in a chaste and discerning heart, or a chaste and well-tested understanding and eloquence. Hebrews 9: 'the blood of Christ will cleanse our conscience from dead works, to serve the living God.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'Christ willingly dwells with the soul that meditates on his passion.'
Tenth, as the same author says, in the same place: partridge eggs, cooked or covered in a bronze vessel with honey, are effective against ulcers of the eyes.

It signifies that firm and well-tested hope of eternal things, together with the sweetness of divine consolations, is of the greatest benefit to holy men, for removing the failings, or blemishes, of the inner man, and for its universal consideration. Romans 8: 'for we are saved by hope. But hope that is seen is not hope; for what a man sees, why does he hope for? But if we hope for that which we see not, we wait for it with patience. Likewise, too, the Spirit helps our weakness.'
The Ordinary Gloss, on the beginning of James: 'in the hope of that good to which you tend, bear all things with an even mind.'
The peacock has these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities.

For first, as Isidore says, and Augustine, in book 21 of the City of God, chapter 4, says he had proven this by experience at Hippo: its flesh is so hard that it does not putrefy or offend the sense of smell even when kept for a year, nor is it easily cooked.

It signifies those firm and rooted in the virtue of evangelical chastity, keeping in themselves the fragrance of good repute, the invincibility of constancy, and the longsuffering of perseverance. 2 Corinthians 2: 'we are the good odor of Christ unto God. Now thanks be to God, who always makes us triumph in Christ Jesus, and manifests the odor of his knowledge by us in every place.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, De ecclesiastica hierarchia Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy: 'a holy life makes precious not only the soul, but also the body.' Likewise there: 'God accepts being loved by the clean.'
Second, as experience proves, and the author says, it has a terrible, demon-like voice, and, as it were —

It signifies detractors and blasphemers. Ecclesiasticus 27: 'much swearing shall fill the head with hair standing on end, and its irreverence will make one stop the ears. The talk of sinners is hateful, and their laughter is in the delights of sin.'
An example is found in Simon Magus, disputing with Peter, as is found in the Itinerary.
Third, as Aristotle puts it, it lives twenty years, and breeds young at the end of three years; then its wings take on their coloring.

It signifies good and persevering, or successive, progress from good to better, in acts and character, according to that saying, Psalm 83: 'they shall go from strength to strength, until the God of gods is seen in Zion.'
Gregory and Bernard, in many places: 'on the way of God, not to advance is to fall back.'
Dionysius: 'it is the property of virtue always and continually to progress.'
Fourth, as the same author says, it sheds its feathers with the first trees that shed their leaves; and its own new feathers are then first born, when the trees begin to bud.
It signifies the renewal of good men, always toward the better, by the example of their elders. 2 Corinthians 4: 'though our outward man is corrupted, yet our inward man is renewed day by day.'

An example is found in the disciples of the holy fathers, of whom Jerome relates, in the book of their Lives, that they always strove to be renewed in Christ, following the example of their teachers; an example too in blessed Maurus and Placidus, under father Benedict, as Gregory relates in book 2 of the Dialogues.

Fifth, as Isidore says, it is a bird that does not love its own offspring. For the male follows the female, and searches out her eggs, so as to break them, so that he may devote himself all the more to his lust. Fearing this, the female hides them, so that they cannot easily be found by him.

It signifies wicked prelates, hindering good, or advancement, in their subjects, which mother Church, taking notice of it, provides against, to the harm of the commonwealth. Proverbs 28: 'a leader void of prudence shall oppress many by his power. As a roaring lion, and a hungry bear, so is a wicked ruler over the poor people.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Against which, Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'learn, prelates, that you ought to be mothers to your subjects, not lords. Grow gentle, lay aside ferocity. And if correction is sometimes needed, let it be fatherly, not tyrannical. Suspend the blows, bring forth the breasts.' Thus far Bernard.

With a crested, serpent-like head, Isidore says, it has a weak and misshapen head, a simple and hidden gait, a modest and upright neck, a sapphire-colored breast, an eyed tail marked and adorned with wondrous beauty of form, and most deformed, wrinkled feet.

It signifies the various conditions of the devil and his ministers, most cunningly and variously transforming themselves into angels of light and apostles of Christ. 2 Corinthians 11: 'for such false apostles are deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ. And no wonder: for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light. It is no great thing, therefore, if his ministers be transformed as the ministers of righteousness, whose end shall be according to their works.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: An example is found in the demon who, crowned with a diadem and adorned with purple, appeared to blessed Martin to deceive him, as is found in his Life, saying that he was Jesus Christ, whom blessed Martin refuted, saying that the Lord Jesus had not foretold he would come in such a form.

Marveling at the beauty of its feathers, it raises them, and arranges them around its head in the manner of a wheel or a circle. But, seeing the ugliness of its feet, it blushes, and, as though forgetting the aforesaid beauty of its feathers, suddenly lowers and casts them down.

It signifies the vainglorious, boasting of and displaying their own beauty and the glory of the world, who, nevertheless, well considering their own frailty and inward foulness, and diligently attending to the truth, are humbled and shrink back from the display of vanity. Job 5: 'visiting your beauty, you shall not sin.'

Augustine, in the book of Confessions: 'O that men would know themselves, and that he who glories, would glory in the Lord! But who reckons up to you his own merits? What does he reckon up to you, my Lord God, but your own gifts?'

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: The peacock swallows its own dung again, begrudging its usefulness to men; for it is very medicinal, but rarely found.
It signifies the greedy and the envious, who not only deny their own vile and superfluous things to the needy, but hide and conceal them from them.

Against which, Ecclesiasticus 29: 'for the commandment's sake, help the poor, and, because of his poverty, send him not away empty. Lose your money for a brother and a friend, and hide it not under a stone, to be lost.'
It is written of holy Edmund, once king of England, that, having refused alms to no poor person, his right arm, with which he gave alms to the poor, has remained incorrupt and whole to this day.
Conversely, it is written of the emperor Decius, and of Julian the Apostate, in the Ecclesiastical History and in the Historia Tripartita, that they held the poor in hatred, and perished damnably.
We have an example too, Luke 16, in the rich and impious feaster, concerning the beggar Lazarus, of how he was buried in hell.
Sparrows are found to have these properties, or conditions, according to the authorities.
For first, as Isidore says, they are called flying things named for their smallness.

They signify the poor not by their own will, or the humble because they can be nothing else, of whom there is a great abundance in the Church, Ecclesiasticus 19: 'there is one that is hindered from sinning through poverty, and in his rest he shall be pricked,' that is, humbled against his will.

bibl.author: Passio sancti Tiburtii (in passione sancti Sebastiani)

cit.quote: Such was Muhammad, as is found in his deeds; such was Julian the Apostate for a time, as is found in the Ecclesiastical History; such was Torquatus, the false familiar of blessed Tiburtius, as is said in the Passion of blessed Tiburtius.
Second, as the same Isidore says, the sparrow is an unstable, garrulous, and troublesome bird, building and living near the dwellings of men.
It signifies fickle men, curious and contentious within the household; against which, 1 Corinthians 11: 'if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor the Church of God.'
'Contend not in words, for it is to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers.'
Augustine, in the book of Confessions: 'the human race is a curious kind, eager to know the life of another, but slow to know its own.'
Philetus and Hermogenes the magician, of blessed Matthew the Apostle, as is found in his passion.
...a bird of great heat and lustfulness; hence its flesh, frequently taken as food, is stimulating to lust, as Constantine says.

It signifies the lustful, who are not only lustful in themselves, but also provoke and drag others into lust; against which: 'but fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not so much as be named among you, as becomes saints,' and so on.
Of such was the harlot Aphrodisia, of whom it is found in the passion of blessed Agatha, that she had nine most base daughters, and so on.
Fourth, as the same Isidore says, the sparrow lays and breeds many young, and is of great skill in raising and nourishing its chicks.
It signifies worldly men, fruitful and eager in the multiplication of children.
'Their seed continues before them, a multitude of kinsmen, and of children's children, in their sight.'
'Their storehouses are full, flowing out of this into that. Their sheep fruitful in young. Their daughters decked out.'
Jair, Judges 11, who had thirty sons riding on thirty ass-colts, and princes over thirty cities.
...ass-colts, who, as is found in Judges 12, had forty sons, and thirty grandsons from them, riding upon seventy asses, Judges 12.
Fifth, as the same Isidore says, it nests in hay and feathers, and keeps its nest clean of dung, casting the droppings of its chicks out of the nest, and compelling them to cast it out too.
It signifies those who despise temporal things, and serve God in poverty, keeping cleanness, and procuring that others keep it too.
'I count all things but loss for the sake of Jesus Christ my Lord, for whom I have counted all things as loss, and I esteem them as dung, that I may gain Christ.'
'I would,' he says, 'that all men were even as myself.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily on 'this is my commandment': 'behold,' he says, 'the elect of God tame the flesh, strengthen the spirit, command the demons, shine with virtues, despise present things, preach the eternal homeland by their voices and their conduct, love it even in dying, and reach it through torments; they can be killed, but cannot be bent.'
Sixth, as the same Isidore says, it feeds its chicks with spiders, worms, and flies.

It signifies base men, who take their pasture from vile, withered, vain, and passing things, and set their life and hope in the superficial, fleeting, and pleasant delights of this life. Hosea 12: 'Ephraim feeds on wind, and follows the burning heat; all the day long he multiplies lying and desolation; he made a covenant with the Assyrians, and carried oil into Egypt.'
Proverbs 10: 'he that trusts to lies, feeds the winds; and the same runs after birds that fly away.'
An example is found in all who set up Haman, Esther 4, and Adonijah, 1 Kings 1, and Absalom, 2 Kings 15, and many others, like Julian the Apostate, and so on.
It eats the poison of henbane without stumbling or harm.

It signifies those who, as though in a state of despair, commit themselves to every danger for the filling of the body, or for the fulfillment of their own intent, of whom the Lord complains, Isaiah 65: 'I have spread forth my hands all the day to an unbelieving people, that walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts. A people that continually provokes me to anger before my face.'

An example is found in two sons of an emperor who, as Jerome puts it in the Lives of the Fathers, stretched nets for hunting in the desert for forty miles, and cornered a certain holy old man, around whom, venting their fury out of ill will, they tried to force him to deny Christ; but they heard from him that they would die the following day by God's judgment, and so it happened.
Eighth, as the same Isidore says, it sometimes suffers and contracts leprosy and the falling sickness.
Mark 9: 'often it cast him into the fire, and into water, to destroy him.'
Such cases are cured only by prayer and fasting, as is found in the same place.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'what is more distant than to withdraw from oneself, and to have, through the intervening heat of worldly lust, a divorce from the saints?'
Ninth, as Aristotle says, the female lives longer than the male.
It signifies certain effeminate and evil men prospering longer, according to the age, than virtuous and good men.
Ecclesiastes 7: 'the just man perishes in his justice, and the wicked man lives a long time in his malice.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, Enarrationes in Psalmos Augustini

cit.quote: But in such cases one must attend to the words of blessed Augustine: 'every wicked man,' he says, 'either lives so that he may be corrected, or so that a good man may be exercised through him.'
The male is jealous for his mate, and is accustomed to fight for her.

It signifies that everyone ought to be jealous, in the higher part of reason, for the lower, lest it be invaded by the enemy. Likewise, that every prelate ought to be jealous for his church, and for every soul entrusted to him, for every advancement in grace, and for its preservation in freedom, truth, and justice.
'Strive for justice for your soul, and contend even unto death for justice, and God will fight your enemies for you.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Morlanensis, De contemptu mundi Bernardi Morlanensis

cit.quote: 'It is not fitting for the handmaid to rule, and the mistress to serve.' And this speaks of the lower and higher part of reason, of which the higher ought to rule universally in the kingdom of the soul, for the preservation of all goodness, holiness, and justice.
Eleventh, as the same Aristotle says, it fears and hates the weasel, and, by crying out and calling loudly, betrays its presence.

It signifies that the devil is to be feared, that is, held in suspicion, hated, and abhorred, and, once his temptation is perceived, that one must cry out to God, and the saints, and the angels, in prayer.
'In the day of my trouble I cried to you, since you heard me.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily for Quinquagesima Sunday: 'the stronger the tumult of carnal thoughts that presses upon us, the more fervently we ought to cry out in prayer.'
The Gloss on Nehemiah, chapter 8: 'prayer is the one refuge against enemies.'
As the author says, to occupy the nests of swallows, it opposes them with beak and bites.

It signifies plunderers, or those who overstep and defraud their brothers; against which, 1 Thessalonians 4: 'that no man overreach, nor circumvent his brother in business, because the Lord is the avenger of all such things, as we have told you before, and testified.'
Laban, Genesis 30 and 31, who so many times deceived the faithful Jacob.
'Sparrows, their chicks, mothers, fathers.'
It signifies pious and charitable men, toward widows, orphans and wards, pilgrims and strangers, the afflicted and the destitute.

Job 29: 'the blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow. I was an eye to the blind, and a foot to the lame. I was the father of the poor. The stranger did not lodge outside, my door was open to the traveler.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: Piety, which, according to the Apostle, is profitable to all things, had filled the heart of Francis with abundant fullness; it drove him upward, through devotion, into God; it transformed him, through compassion, into Christ; it inclined him, through condescension, toward his neighbor; it refigured him, through reconciliation with the other creatures, back to the state of innocence.
A crowd of sparrows call one another mutually, and, to free one that has been captured, hasten and rush as best they can.
It signifies how much diligence and charity one man ought to have for another, in a time of adversity and danger.
Proverbs 6: 'run about, hasten, stir up your friend.'
'Deliver them that are led to death, and cease not to deliver them that are drawn to destruction.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, De diversis questionibus octoginta tribus

cit.quote: Augustine, book 83 of Questions: 'nothing so proves a friend as bearing a friend's burden.'

An example is found in two philosopher friends, of whom blessed Ambrose writes in the book On Holy Virginity, that when one of them had been condemned, and, on the sabbath day of his beheading, was without doubt awaiting and desiring to arrange matters concerning his house and his children in person, the other willingly entered prison to die in his place, if he did not return. But since he faithfully returned, while his substitute was being led to execution, it happened that the great faith and friendship of both was reported at once to the emperor, who was nearby in his palace; he at once absolved the condemned man, and set both of them as friends at his side, saying that it befitted an emperor to have such friends.

An example is found likewise in blessed Paulinus, bishop of Nola, who gave himself up in place of a widow's son, as blessed Gregory relates in book 3 of the Dialogues, chapter 1, and consequently led back all the other captives too.
The ostrich is found to have these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities.
For first, as Isidore says, it took its name from a Greek word, since it has the body of an animal, yet has feathers as a bird does, and two feet, and a beak like a bird.

...hypocrites, who are carnal and wish to seem spiritual, seeking heavenly things by outward show of contemplation and devotion, Titus 1: 'they profess that they know God, but in their works they deny him, being abominable, and incredulous.'
'Having an appearance indeed of godliness, but denying the power thereof.'

bibl.author: Passio sancti Tiburtii (in passione sancti Sebastiani)

cit.quote: Such were Muhammad, as is found in his deeds, and Nicholas, the newcomer from Antioch, as is found in his errors, and Torquatus, as is found in the Passion of blessed Tiburtius, who, under the cloak of virtue, advanced the cause of falsehood.
Second, as the same Isidore states, because of the heaviness of its body, it is not lifted into the air along with other birds.

It signifies those who love, or follow, carnal indulgences and bodily rest, and cannot rise with spiritual men to divine things, Proverbs 20: 'wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness riotous; whosoever is delighted therewith shall not be wise.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Augustine, On the Spirit and the Soul: 'bodily delight hinders the knowledge of spiritual good'; against which, Ecclesiastes 2: 'I thought in my heart to withdraw my flesh from wine, that I might turn my mind to wisdom, and might avoid folly.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: It is sung of blessed Martin, a man of sober life, as is found in his Life, that, 'his eyes and hands always intent upon heaven, he never relaxed his unconquered spirit from prayer.'

Likewise it is read of blessed Francis, his senses wholly mortified, that he was suspended wholly in God, even lifted bodily from the earth, a heavenly brightness surrounding him and the place where he prayed, in a marvelous manner, seen at night by his companions in the wilderness.
Third, as the same Isidore states, it lays eggs like a bird, but neglects to warm them; yet, cast into the sand, they are quickened by the warmth of the dust.
It signifies negligent prelates: 'like the ostrich, she leaves her eggs on the earth, and forgets that the foot may tread upon them, or that the beasts of the field may crush them.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: 'She is hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers'; against which blessed Martin used to say, as is found in his Life: 'Lord, if I am still necessary to your people, I do not refuse the labor on their account.'
The Apostle says something similar, Philippians 1.
Fourth, as Aristotle says, it is of such heat that it swallows and consumes iron.

It signifies those in the Church, or a congregation, who have an immoderate zeal, so much so that sometimes it even casts down the strong, and leads to spiritual change and consumption. Romans 10: 'I bear them witness that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'Let charity inflame the zealous man, knowledge inform him, constancy make him firm. Let him be fervent, let him be circumspect, let him be unconquered. Lest you be seduced by the spirit of lying, let Christ, the truth, shine for you; lest you be led away by the glory of the world or by pleasures, let the wisdom of Christ be sweet to you; lest you be wearied by adversities, let Christ, the power of God, strengthen you.'

Fifth, as Avicenna says, since it is a bird of good size, it lays very large eggs with very hard shells, so that, while occupied in generating them, the heat may be tempered, and excessive heat not be the cause of their dying too quickly.

It signifies the great hope of eternal glory, in the present life, which, together with sobriety of life and zeal, advances holy men, out of charity, toward the bringing forth of holy works. Titus 3: 'looking for the blessed hope, and coming of the glory of the great God and our savior Jesus Christ; let us live soberly, and justly, and godly, in this world.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia, and elsewhere: 'the holy men of God lead their life in patience, but their death in desire.'

Blessed Jerome relates an example, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, of a certain holy father who laughed three times as he was dying, since those attending him feared death, while he himself went joyfully to his rest.
Sixth, as the same author says, it has many feathers in the lower part of its body.

It signifies those abounding in delights and pleasures, as regards sense, and especially generation, whose voice is, as in Wisdom: 'come, let us enjoy the good things that are present. Let us crown ourselves with roses. Let no meadow be free from our luxury. For this is our portion, and this our lot.'
Such men can in no way savor divine things, being wholly bent toward earthly ones.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities never deserve to know divine things.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: As Gregory says, on Job: its feather is like the feathers of the heron and the hawk in color, but not in power. 'For it has the likeness of a feather, but lacks the swiftness of flight'; it raises its wings for flight, but is nonetheless in no way lifted from the earth into the air; 'it is clothed with sparse feathers, and is weighed down in its great body.'
It signifies those who make a show of the appearance of a pig, or a sow: 'a beautiful and foolish woman.'

bibl.author: Hugo de Sancto Victore, De meditatione Hugonis de Sancto Victore

cit.quote: 'The reason why so few advance is this: that all have their eye turned outward, toward the appearance of the work, and not inward, toward the profit of virtue.'
'Favor is deceitful, and beauty is vain,' and so on. Last chapter of Proverbs.

Eighth, as the same Gregory says, when the time comes for it to lay eggs, it lifts its eyes to the Pleiades; for it lays no eggs except when that constellation rises or ascends. But when it sees those stars, around the month of June, it lays then.

It signifies holy men who, in all the good things they do, always hold and lift their intentions, vows, and affections toward heaven. Colossians 3: 'all whatsoever you do, in word or in work, do all in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks always to God the Father.'

bibl.author: Hugo de Sancto Victore, De virtute orandi Hugonis de Sancto Victore

cit.quote: 'God is in no way better inclined to hear us than when the mind turns to him with the whole affection of devotion.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: An example is found in blessed Martin who, as is found in his Life, 'with eyes and hands always intent on heaven, did not relax his unconquered spirit from prayer.'
Ninth, as the same Gregory says, once it has laid its eggs, it hides them in the sand, and covers them, and forgets, and so never returns to them.

It signifies those who beget spiritual sons or daughters in the Church, and afterward take no care for their advancement or state; against which: 'my little children, of whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you.'
'We became, in the midst of you, as a nurse cherishing her children.'
An example is found in blessed John the Evangelist, as is found in his Life and Acts, of how he cherished those he converted, especially the young robber he had converted.
'Chicks.'
It signifies those who recognize and cherish their own, or even others, in prosperity, but not in adversity, according to that saying, Psalm 48: 'he will praise you when you shall do well to him.'
The Gloss, there: 'praise that comes from prosperity is suspect.'
Ecclesiasticus 12: 'a friend shall not be known in prosperity, and an enemy shall not be hidden in adversity.'

Eleventh, as the author says, it naturally hates the horse, and is so opposed to it that the horse cannot see it without terror. And if the horse should meet it, it raises its wings as against an enemy, and, with the beating of its wings, forces it, as it were, to flee.

It signifies that the wicked rise up against the good, and cannot bear to see them, and, with all the presumption they can muster, lead them to confusion. 2 Timothy 3: 'now as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith. But they shall proceed no further; for their folly shall be manifest to all, as theirs also was.'

Chrysostom, in the sermon for the third Sunday in Lent: 'the wicked cannot bear to see what is good. The wicked do not wish the better man to live, lest they, degenerate, should have to bear reproaches for their own baseness; so the life of the good is a torment to the very worst.'

div.head: Cap. 36: De papagallo seu de psittaco

cit.quote: The parrot is a bird of which blessed Ambrose writes, in the Hexameron, book 5, chapters 17 and 26, that it is a bird having a voice clearly formed in the manner of a man's. For he says thus: 'from where do I get the voices of a parrot?'; and again: 'how clearly formed is the parrot's voice!'

It signifies, by this bird, with its green color known to all and its red beak, the evangelical preachers, faithfully shining forth in the catholic faith, speaking with the fervor of the Holy Spirit, and clearly pronouncing the words of God to all, according to Habakkuk 2: 'the just man lives by his faith.'
Ecclesiasticus 48: 'his word burned like a torch.'
And in Psalm 18: 'their sound has gone forth into all the earth,' and so on.

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, Epistole Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Dionysius, in the letter to Timothy on the death of Peter and Paul, calls Paul the loud-sounding trumpet of all the churches.
The turtledove has these properties, or meanings, according to the authorities.
For first, as Isidore says, it is so named from its mournful and groaning voice.

It signifies holy or religious men, always groaning and sighing for eternal things. Romans 8: 'ourselves also, having the first-fruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption of the sons of God.'
It is written of blessed [Dominic] that he made of his eyes, as it were, a fountain of tears, and those tears were his bread day and night.
It is also written of blessed Francis that he found no consolation except in tears, on account of which he lost his eyesight before his time.
Second, as the same Isidore says, it is, like the dove, simple, but far less cheerful.

It signifies certain simple men in the Church, or religious, little children in the malice of gall, but refreshed with the sweetness of charity and love, and of heavenly consolation. 1 Corinthians 14: 'do not become children in sense, but in malice be children; but in sense be perfect.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: For this reason Ambrose says, on Luke, that 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot savor divine things.'

It is called a chaste bird, from its character, or its movements, since it is a companion of chastity; for, once it has lost its mate, it seeks no other union, walks and chooses solitary places, and, mindful of its former companionship, always groans, and greatly flees the company of men.

It signifies, for religious men, true lovers of chastity, driving themselves upward toward heavenly things alone, once earthly company is lost, worldly vanities renounced. 2 Corinthians 6: 'in all things let us exhibit ourselves as the ministers of God,' and so on, 'in chastity, in sweetness, in the Holy Spirit. As chastised, and not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing.'

Jerome, to the virgin Demetrias: 'happy is that conscience of Christ, and blessed the virginity, in whose heart, besides the love of Christ, which is wisdom, chastity, patience, and justice, and the other virtues, no other love dwells, nor does it ever sigh at the remembrance of a man, nor desire to see one whom, once seen, it would be unwilling to let go.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Augustine, in the book On the Spirit and the Soul: 'nothing is more excellent, for a blessed life, than to turn within oneself, and be made a stranger to desires.'

Fourth, as the same Isidore says, it comes down to men's gardens, where it seeks food for itself; but once it has obtained food, it is accustomed to seek again the mountain ridges and the secret places of the woods.

It signifies contemplatives, given continually to heavenly things, apart from the moments needed for taking necessities. Luke 2: 'this widow lived to eighty-four years, who did not depart from the temple, serving God with fastings and prayers, night and day.'

An example is found in blessed Benedict, book 2 of Gregory's Dialogues, who remained three years in a cave, unknown except to a Roman monk, contemplating eternal things, and sighing for the heavenly, meditating on divine things, and spurning earthly ones.

Fifth, as the same Isidore says, it arrives in springtime, and, with a plaintive voice, announces and reveals the newness of the coming season. But in winter it loses its feathers, and then hides itself in the hollows of tree-trunks.

It signifies those who gladly and lovingly preach and announce to others, with sweet-flowing and most pure words, the pleasantness of the eternal, ever-green and ever-flowering paradise. But in this wretched present life they deprive themselves of every pleasure, and remove themselves from all the world's delights and vanities.

And this is what is said, Song of Songs 2: 'the flowers have appeared in our land, the time of pruning has come; the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land; the fig tree has put forth her green figs.'

It is sung of blessed Augustine, and is found in book 9 of the Confessions, that, having received the grace of baptism, he, together with his mother, at the mouth of the Tiber, spoke together, alone, most sweetly. And they reached out, with the mouth of the heart, together, toward the supernal streams of the fountain of life. And this world grew worthless amid their words and its delights. Then she said to her son: 'nothing now delights me in this life, since, having already scorned earthly happiness, I now see a servant of Christ.'

As Aristotle says, around springtime, its feathers regrown, coming out from the hidden places where it had lain, it builds fitting places for breeding, in which it broods over its eggs, breeds, and nourishes its chicks.

It signifies religious men who, at a fixed time, devote themselves mainly to solitude, and come forth at fixed times to give examples for the fruitfulness and salvation of souls, or for the conversion of sinners and the strengthening of the weak. 2 Corinthians 5: 'for whether we be transported in mind, it is to God; or whether we be sober, it is for you. For the charity of Christ presses us.'

Augustine, book 10 of the Confessions: 'terrified by my sins, and weighed down by the mass of my misery, I had turned this over in my heart, and had considered flight into solitude, but you forbade me, Lord, through your apostle, saying: therefore Christ died for all, that they who live may now not live to themselves, but to him who died for all.'
It is also sung of blessed Augustine: 'after his mother's death, Augustine returned to his own lands, where, devoting himself to holy readings and prayers, he wrote books and taught the unlearned.'
...blessed Ambrose, as is found in the Confessions of Augustine.
It lives and broods for fifteen years.

It signifies that contemplatives live and delight in mind according to the fifteen perfect and graduated ascents of the virtues, above the mind, which are mystically contained in the canticle of the fifteen degrees in the Psalter. Psalm 83: 'blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has disposed ascensions in his heart, in the vale of tears, in the place which he has set.'
'For the lawgiver will give a blessing, they shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion.'

Blessed Jerome relates an example, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, of twelve hermits dwelling near each other in the desert, who, once gathered together, said to one another what each meditated on chiefly, of whom the eighth said: 'I, turning over in my mind the empyrean heaven, contemplate the Lord of glory, shining, in the midst of the intellectual powers, above them all.' The others too, one by one, declared their own graces, in a similar but different way.

Eighth, as the same Aristotle says, it never descends upon a foul thing, nor upon a carcass; for it does not feed on carrion, but seeks, for its own food and that of its young, a few clean grains, and gathers them in clean places, where it lives.

It signifies holy men, leading their lives in poverty and cleanness, from their own just labor, never from another's, or from something base or basely acquired: 'and having food, and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content.'
Ephesians 4: 'he that stole, let him now steal no more; but rather let him labor, working with his hands, that he may have something to give to him that suffers need.'
Peter, to Clement, in the Itinerary: 'bread alone, with olives, and rarely also with vegetables, is my usual food. As for clothing, this that you see is a tunic with a cloak,' and so on.
Ninth, as the same Aristotle says, while other birds cry out, it groans.
It signifies the penitent man who, while worldly men exult, devotes himself to groaning. 'Like the young of the swallow, so will I cry, and I will meditate like a dove.'
'We groan, meditating like doves.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: It is written of blessed Francis, in his Life, that 'he sought solitary places, friendly to sorrow, in which, with unspeakable groanings, he ceaselessly besought God, and, after a long persistence in prayer, deserved to be heard by the Lord.'
As the same Aristotle says, it builds its nest from small dry sticks, or twigs, low, poor, and stiff.

It signifies the evangelical man, content with a small and despised dwelling. Ecclesiasticus 29: 'better is the living of a poor man under a shelter of boards, than sumptuous fare,' and so on; there too: 'let a little be pleasing to you instead of much,' and so on.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Vita sancti Hilarionis abbatis in Palestina Hieronymi

cit.quote: An example is found in blessed Hilarion, of whom blessed Jerome writes, in his Life, that he lay on a bed of rushes until his death, and his dwelling was so small and narrow that it seemed more a tomb than a hut.
Once its mate has died, it never again settles on a green branch, nor drinks water unless it is troubled.

It signifies that a Christian, considering the death of Christ, who is joined and conformed to us in humanity, should never wish to rejoice in a worldly way, but always wish, in his inmost heart, to be transformed, in compassion, toward the crucified one. Philippians 3: 'for Christ's sake, I have counted all things as loss; and I esteem them as dung.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: It is written of blessed Francis, in his Life, that he lamented Christ's passion as though it were always set before him, gazing at the crucified one with groaning mind and groaning eyes, and counted this whole universe as nothing.

As Constantine says, the chicks of the turtledove are hot and moist, which their heaviness in flying attests; but, once they begin to fly, they lose that heaviness, and their flesh becomes lighter and more agreeable to digest.

It signifies those who, although prone by nature to wrath and lust, procure for themselves gentleness and chastity through holy desires and diligent exercise of the virtues, and heavenly increase of lofty merits. Matthew: 'from the days of John the Baptist, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent bear it away.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, De officiis ministrorum Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Ambrose, On the Duties of Ministers, and elsewhere: 'everyone claims dignity for himself by grace, not by nature; by virtue, not by nobility of birth.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: Bernard, to Eugenius: 'the lineage of the apostles is proven noble by nothing else than the nobility of their character.'

bibl.author: Iohannes Chrysostomus, Homilie super Mattheum Iohannis Chrysostomi

cit.quote: Chrysostom, on Matthew, homily 44: 'there is one true nobility, namely, to do the will of God.'
Thirteenth, as the same Constantine puts it, the blood of its right wing is medicinal, just as the blood of the swallow and of the dove.
It signifies that the blood of Christ's passion is a medicine against all spiritual infirmities. Hebrews 9: 'the blood of Christ will cleanse our conscience from dead works, to serve the living God.'
Augustine, in the sermon On a Single Martyr: 'whomever the cunning of Satan has bitten, let him look upon Christ hanging on the wood; for there death was slain; the Lord lives forever.'
The vulture is found, according to the doctors, to have these properties, or conditions.
For first, as Isidore says, it is so named from its slow flight, as it were flying slowly. For, because of the great bulk of its flesh, it does not have swift flight.

It signifies those who become slow and lazy in rising toward God, or toward worthy works, on account of the abundance of carnality within them, which drives away from itself the spirit of grace. Wisdom 1: 'wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins.
