For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful, and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding.'
'For the corruptible body is a load upon the soul, and the earthly habitation presses down the mind that muses upon many things.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Augustine, On the Spirit and the Soul: 'bodily delight hinders the knowledge of spiritual good.'
Augustine, Against Julian: 'the movement of pleasure, being greatest, is likewise most hostile to lust; for bodily delight cannot agree with understanding.'

Second, as the same Isidore says, and blessed Ambrose in the Hexameron, vultures are said not to mate, but to conceive and be conceived, and to beget and be born, without coupling. For they do this by scent alone.

They signify virgins, begotten and begetting for God, without the foulness of carnal union, in fruits of the everlasting flowering and sweet-smelling delights of paradise. Ecclesiasticus 15: 'he that is a keeper of the law of justice shall get the mastery of her, and she will meet him as an honorable mother, and will receive him as a wife married of a virgin.'
'Come over to me,' says the Blessed Virgin Mary, 'all you that desire me, and be filled with my fruits. I am the mother of fair love.'

Fulgentius, in the sermon On All Saints, third lesson: 'the blessed mother of God, ever Virgin Mary, temple of the Lord, sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, virgin before childbirth and virgin after childbirth; forming a godly people, she admonished them to spurn the perishing luxuries of the world, to turn away from the enticements of mortal nature, and to keep the purity of the flesh, together with the honor of virginity, within the lodgings of the heart, and affirmed that she was the queen of all virtues, the fruit of everlasting salvation, and a companion of the angels, by her own examples, so that a multitude of both sexes might imitate her.'
Third, as Isidore puts it, vultures live for a hundred years.
They signify perseverance in justice, even to the palm of martyrdom. Ecclesiasticus 4: 'strive for justice for your soul, and contend even unto death for justice.'

...martyrs, on account of the fullness of the life they have attained, or the perfect contempt of death, or the ready flight from the left hand of this life to the right hand of the homeland; virgins, on account of leisure and the perfection of integrity, by which they do not fight against the habit of the flesh; widows, in whom there is a great struggle, lest they be overcome by desire.

But Jerome, in the Apology to Pammachius, treating this same saying, speaks thus: 'thirty is referred to marriage, since the very joining of the fingers, as though embracing and binding itself in a soft kiss, marks the husband and the wife. But sixty is referred to widows, since they are placed in tribulation and distress; hence they are pressed down by the higher finger; and the greater the difficulty of abstaining from the enticements of a pleasure once known, the greater the reward. Further — I beg the diligent reader to attend — the number a hundred is transferred from the left hand to the right, and, with these same fingers, though not the same hand, by which married women and widows are signified on the left, it forms a circle, expressing the crown of virginity.' And below, in the same place: 'and certainly we have been much more indulgent toward marriage than almost all the Latin and Greek commentators, who refer the number a hundred to martyrs, sixty to virgins, but thirty to widows. And so it happens that husbands are excluded from the good earth and the seed of the father of the household.' Thus far Jerome. Whichever of these two ways, then, we wish to apply our moral reading of the hundred, we have, behold, a fitting path.

Fourth, as Pliny says, it is unkind toward its own young, like the kite too. For when it sees them growing fat, it strikes them with beak and feet, so that they become lean from the pain of the bites.

It signifies those who grow sad at the good fortune, or prosperous successes, of an Abel-like brother, as Cain did concerning Abel, Genesis 4, and the brothers of Joseph, Genesis 37; against which, 'charity is kind; it seeks not its own. It does not rejoice at iniquity, but rejoices with the truth.'
John the Evangelist, who rejoiced most of all when he felt his children growing in Christ, as is found near the beginning of 2 John and in the accounts of his deeds.

Fifth, as the same Pliny says, vultures are especially strong in their sense of smell; hence they perceive the smell of carcasses from far off. For those existing beyond the sea perceive them on this side, and conversely; hence an army is followed by vulture upon vulture, as it were, to be sated on the corpses of men as well as horses. According to the augurs, too, when many vultures gather and fly about, it is an omen of a coming battle, which they foresee, by some hidden natural sense, is going to happen.

It signifies certain gluttons, or even entertainers, who, wherever weddings, or courts, or carnal feasts take place, or wherever they know there is an opportunity to fill their belly, or gain some temporal profit, run there anxiously and gorge themselves; and when they multiply, it is a sign of the multiplication of crimes, and, consequently, of infernal punishments. The letter of Jude: 'these are spots in their banquets, feasting together without fear, feeding themselves, clouds without water, which are carried about by the winds; to whom the storm of darkness is reserved forever.'
Bernard, in his sermons: 'the pleasure of gluttony, so highly esteemed today, occupies scarcely the breadth of two fingers.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Likewise, Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'the life of men is midway between the life of angels and of cattle, so that those who savor according to the spirit are made like the angels, but those who feel according to the flesh are joined with the beasts.'
'Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he has been compared to senseless cattle, and made like to them.'
As Aristotle says, the vulture fights with the heron, and flies over it, and, when it defeats it, it dies.

It signifies attackers of good men, deserving, by this very act, eternal death, and sometimes temporal death too, as is clear in the two companies of fifty men, sent to seize Elijah, who was troubling them, devoured by fire from heaven, 2 Kings 1.
An example is found in the tyrant Aegeas, adversary of blessed Andrew, and the tyrant Paschasius, adversary of blessed Lucy, and many others, as is found in the Ecclesiastical Acts.
...a bird of raw flesh, and so it fights against other birds for food.

It signifies detractors, attacking holy men out of envy, or to fulfill their own evil will. Micah 3: 'they bite with their teeth, and preach peace; and if any man gives not something for their mouths, they prepare war against him.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'A cursed tongue strikes charity in all who hear it, and, as far as lies in it, thoroughly kills and extinguishes it.'

Eighth, as Aristotle says, it hunts from noon until night, and rests from sunrise until that hour; and when it grows old, its beak lengthens above, and curves at the tip, and finally it dies of hunger.

It signifies the greedy, who press after temporal gains from youth even to death, and, never satisfied, in the end come to eternal damnation. Ecclesiastes 4: 'considering, I found also another vanity under the sun: there is but one, and he has not a second, no child, nor brother, and yet he ceases not to labor, neither are his eyes satisfied with riches; neither does he reflect, saying: for whom do I labor, and defraud my soul of good things?'
Psalm 75: 'they have slept their sleep; and all the men of riches have found nothing in their hands.'
Luke 16, of him who, as the Church sings, asked for a drop of water, since he had denied crumbs of bread to Lazarus the beggar.

As the same Aristotle says, when it has some food left over, it does not leave anything for other birds, as the eagle does, but stores it in the nest, to feed its chicks, since it does not easily obtain food.

It signifies the rich, and men of this kind, who leave nothing for the poor, and are unwilling even to give their leftovers to needy neighbors, but turn everything to their own private benefit and carnal love, saying that temporal goods of this kind are not easily gotten. Job 15: 'there was nothing left of his food. Therefore nothing of his goods shall remain.'

...the emperor Decius, and Julian the Apostate, who, as history relates, held the poor in hatred, and had compassion on no one afflicted — indeed, they added to their affliction, whereas to persecute the poor is the height of savagery, as the Gloss says on Psalm 69: 'O God, come to my assistance.'
As the same Aristotle says, it nests on high mountains and in dense groves.

It signifies the proud and the ambitious, walking in things great and marvelous, above themselves. Isaiah 14: 'I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God, I will sit in the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the north.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs, and in his sermons and letters: 'every proud man is utterly unbearable; his manner of dress is excessive, his gait pompous, his neck stiff, he strives from a loftier place, and desires to be preferred to his betters; he boasts of his own opinions and his own deeds, and keeps no reverence in his service.'
Eleventh, as the same Aristotle says, if it sees anything flying around its young, it strikes it with its beak, and drives it off.

It signifies those who claim their goods as their own private possession, denying them to the common charity of their neighbors. Philippians 2: 'for all seek the things that are their own, not the things that are Jesus Christ's.'
Nabal of Carmel, 1 Kings 25, who, for this reason, died an evil death.
Such were Antiochus, 2 Maccabees 7, and Ahab, 1 Kings 17, and many others.

As the same Aristotle says, it feeds its chicks until they can fly, and then casts them from the nest, and forbids them to approach that place, nor does it allow one pair of vultures to enter the place of another.

It signifies those who, though they could be hospitable, refuse to be, and, once they have fed the poor man even once, no longer wish to see him again; against which: 'let brotherly charity remain among you, and forget not hospitality, for by this some, unknowingly, have received angels as guests.'

Against those unwilling to help travelers, blessed Jerome relates, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, that there was a man and his wife who divided all their substance and gain among the poor: first, among travelers; second, for their own use; third, among those living in virginity. They lay clothed in sackcloth at night, and it was revealed to two holy fathers, who wished to know their own merits, that they had not attained their measure.

There is a certain species of river-bird called the almachar, which fears the vulture, and so flees to the water, while the vulture flies around at a distance; and, since it has keen eyes, it watches for when that bird leaves the water, and then, if it can, seizes it.

It signifies the cunning of the devil, by which he strives to overcome the men of God, according to that saying, 1 Peter 5: 'be sober, and watch, because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goes about, seeking whom he may devour.'

bibl.author: Leo Magnus, Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: Pope Leo, in the sermon On the Circumcision: 'the ancient enemy does not cease to press on, so as to corrupt, by whatever means, the faith of Christians, or the faithful. He knows to whom he should offer the incitements of lust, the heat of desire; to whom he should pour in the poison of envy; to whom he should show the poisons of deceit. He knows whom to deceive with joy, whom to trouble with sorrow. He has certain ones among them whom he has bound to himself so tightly that he makes use of their wits and their tongues for the deception of others.'
As the same author says, it is a very foul-smelling and unclean bird.

It signifies the unclean life of the lustful and the wanton. Philippians 3: 'for many walk, of whom I have told you often (and now tell you weeping), that they are enemies of the cross of Christ; whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.' Such men cannot grasp or savor divine or heavenly and intellectual things.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot know divine things.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs, and elsewhere: 'divine consolation is a delicate thing, which is not given to those who possess what belongs to another.'
As the same author says, its flesh is very hard, of bad flavor and heavy odor, and so is useless for food.

It signifies the life of certain evil, or depraved and perverse men, whose life is of bad composition in conscience, of bad edification in life, and of bad reputation in fame, and so fruitless in every way for the Church. 2 Timothy 2: 'of whom is Philetus and Hymenaeus, who have fallen from the truth, saying that the resurrection is past already, and have subverted the faith of some. But the sure foundation of God stands firm, having this seal: the Lord knows who are his.'

bibl.author: Passio sancti Tiburtii (in passione sancti Sebastiani)

cit.quote: Nicholas, the newcomer from Antioch, and Torquatus, the betrayer of Tiburtius, Julian the Apostate, and Muhammad, and similar members of the devil, of whom their own accounts speak.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: As Gregory says, on Job, it easily comes down to earth for a carcass, but, once it has come down from the earth, it scarcely rises again.

It signifies money to hypocrites, or the greedy, who, for a small thing, seek earthly gain, and, once the desire or pursuit of earthly things has taken root in their affections, scarcely return to salutary things. Ecclesiasticus 10: 'there is not a more wicked thing than to love money; for such a one sets even his own soul to sale, since, while he lives, he has cast away his innermost parts.'

Concerning this, blessed Jerome relates, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, that there was a certain holy gardener who, apart from what he needed for his own use, spent all his gains on the poor, and was healthy. And the devil put into his heart the desire to gather money, lest he perhaps fall ill and be in want; and afterward he did fall ill, and his foot was to be cut off, unless, led by penitence, he was healed by God before the physician arrived.
As the same author says, flying high, it spies a carcass far below, and, for love of the carcass, lowers itself from the height of the air.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: It signifies the Son of God Most High, according to blessed Gregory in the Moralia, who, existing in the bosom of the Father, and, seeing the human race made, as it were, a corpse because of Adam's sin, though he was in the form of God, out of pity took flesh from the Virgin, and came down to it, to incorporate it into himself. But while he was drawing it to himself, the adversaries of the people who came upon him, namely the Jews, seized him like a vulture, and killed him, as though blind, not turning aside, nor caring to know, the savior who was working salvation in the midst of their land.

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, Enarrationes in Psalmos Augustini

cit.quote: Indeed, according to Augustine, on the Psalms, they, as though feverish with a great madness, raged against the physician who had come to heal them.

Job 28 says, of the Jewish people: 'the bird has not known the path, neither has the eye of the vulture beheld it,' since that blinded people scorned to turn aside to the ways of Christ, walking on earth in the manner of an angel, always lifted toward heavenly things, and did not care to consider his intention and his affection, in the manner of a vulture striving to incorporate the human race into himself and draw it to himself.
But whence they thought to cast him down, from there they exalted him, since, Proverbs 21: 'there is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord.'
'Jesus, crowned with glory and honor, because of the suffering of death.'

Eighteenth, as the same author says, when it is hindered by something, it beats its wings against the wind, and so, by the wind's help rather than its own labor, lifts itself from the depths into the air.

It signifies contemplative and holy men who, enduring at times the troubles of temptations, and recognizing their own frailty, commit themselves entirely to the grace of the Holy Spirit, by whose worthy inspiration, lifted above the level of the mind toward heavenly things with all their desires, they overcome the depths of those very temptations, and triumph over all their trials. 2 Corinthians 2: 'let us not be deceived by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his devices. Now thanks be to God, who always makes us triumph in Christ Jesus.'
2 Corinthians 1: 'in all things we overcome, because of him that has loved us.'

The Master relates, in the Summa of Vices, that when a certain holy man was tempted with the sin of fornication, and could resist no longer, he prostrated himself before the crucifix, and said: 'the earth, or fortress, of my body, which I hold from you, I can no longer defend. I return it to you. You defend it.' And at once the temptation was overcome, and so the tempter withdrew, confounded.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Among birds, the vulture is opposed to serpents. For if its feathers are burned, they drive off serpents with their smell. Its heart, too, keeps those who carry it safe from serpents and wild beasts. Its heart, likewise, bound in the skin of a lion or a wolf, drives off demons. Its feather, bound to the left foot of a woman in labor, quickly delivers her; but it ought to be loosened more quickly once the child begins to come forth, lest the afterbirth follow with it. An ointment made from the vulture's fat and oil of iris heals the sinews, and cures beasts of burden. Its right foot, bound to a painful left foot, heals it; likewise, the left heals the right. Its tongue, drawn out without iron and hung on the neck in a new cloth, is said to make a man pleasing, so as to obtain from another whatever he asks. The ash of its burned bones, mixed with celandine, heals the diseases of animals. Its blood, with the herb 'carabeote' and celandine, heals leprosy. Thus far Pliny, in the said book.

It signifies that holy men, and whatever is in their souls and bodies, and even in their garments and relics, fight for God and for truth, and are opposed to the devil and to all malice, or iniquity, and to every spiritual infirmity. Acts 5: 'and the multitude of men and women who believed in the Lord was more increased, so that they brought forth the sick into the streets, and laid them on beds and couches, that when Peter came, his shadow at the least might overshadow any of them, and they might be delivered from their infirmities. And there came also together a multitude out of the neighboring cities to Jerusalem, bringing sick persons, and such as were troubled with unclean spirits, who were all healed.'

'God worked no small miracles by the hand of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs and aprons were brought from his body to the sick, and the diseases departed from them, and the wicked spirits went out of them.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'do you wish to know the gifts of God? The garments of Paul were a terror to demons.'
Augustine, in the Confessions: 'let my tongue, Lord, and whatever I think, know, savor, and write, serve you.'
The screech-owl is found, according to the authorities, to have these conditions, or properties.
For first, as Isidore says, it is named from its wailing, or rather its screeching. For it screeches a great deal, especially by night, over buildings.

It signifies those who always lament and complain of poverty, or some other adversity, always laboring for their own relief, whom, on account of their persistence, one must sometimes satisfy. Luke 18: 'there was a judge in a certain city, who feared not God, nor regarded man. And there was a certain widow in that city, and she came to him, saying: avenge me of my adversary. And he would not for a long time. But afterward he said within himself: although I fear not God, nor regard man, yet because this widow is troublesome to me, I will avenge her, lest continually coming, she weary me.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Iohannis Eleemosynarii episcopi Alexandrie

cit.quote: An example is found in those who, feigning themselves poor, deceived John the Almsgiver, the patriarch, as is related in his Life, and, because of their persistence, received something from him, but were nonetheless justly judged by divine judgment, as is found in the accounts of his deeds.
Second, as the same Isidore says, this bird, among the augurs, when it screeches a great deal, portends adversity; but, when silent, portends prosperity.

It signifies detractors who, when they detract greatly, bring, or foreshadow, their own damnation; but when they hold back, or restrain themselves, they do themselves good, and deserve to have God propitious to them.
For this reason the wise man says, Proverbs 24: 'my son, fear God, and the king, and have no fellowship with detractors, for their destruction shall rise suddenly, and who knows the ruin of both?'
'The north wind drives away rain, as does a sad countenance a backbiting tongue.'
'He that detracts from anything binds himself for the future, but he that fears the commandment shall dwell in peace.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'A heart bitter with the gall of envy cannot scatter, through the instrument of the tongue, anything but bitter things. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks; and there are two kinds of this plague,' and so on. Thus far Bernard, in the same place.
As the same Isidore says, its voice is generally, according to the augurs, unlucky and hostile.

It signifies certain talkative men, multiplying words without reason, and bringing on others a certain misfortune, or a heavy tedium. Ecclesiasticus 27: 'much swearing shall fill the head with hair standing on end, and its irreverence will make one stop the ears. The talk of sinners is hateful, and their laughter is in the delights of sin.'
An example is found in Simon Magus, of whom the Itinerary speaks, and in many other similar men, in the Old Testament and in the New.
The hoopoe is found to have these conditions, or properties.
As Isidore says, it is a bird helmeted with crests rising from its head.
It signifies the proud, and those who make a show of themselves.

An example is found in the illustrious Antiochus, 1 Maccabees 1; against which, Esther 14: 'you know, Lord, that I abhor the sign of my pride, which is upon my head in the days of my public appearance, and detest it like a cloth stained with menstrual blood.'
It is written of blessed Bernard that he considered every honor shown to him as belonging equally to another.

Second, as the same Isidore says, it is a bird beautiful in its feathers and varied in color, but most filthy in its deeds. For it eats human dung, and dwells among dung-heaps or tombs, and therefore always stinks.
It signifies beasts of burden, that is, luxurious men appearing beautiful in their garments, but foul and stinking in soul and body, Joel 1: 'the beasts have rotted in their own dung.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'for beasts to rot in their own dung is for carnal men to end their life in the stench of luxury.'

Third, as the philosophers say, and as Isidore states, when it grows old, so that it can neither see nor fly, its chicks pluck out its weakened feathers, and anoint its eyes with the juices of herbs, and warm it beneath their wings until its feathers grow back. And so, fully renewed, it flies and sees clearly, just as they themselves do.

It signifies that works of piety are to be devoted, with great zeal, to one's parents. Ecclesiasticus 3: 'he that fears the Lord honors his parents, and will serve them as his masters that brought him into the world,' and so on.
Jerome, in a certain letter: 'love the superior of the monastery as a father, esteem him as a teacher, believe whatever he shall tell you.'
The bat is found to have these properties, or conditions, according to the authorities.
For first, as Isidore says, and as Ambrose touches on in the Hexameron, it took its name from the time of day, since, being blind, it flies about in the twilight of evening.

It signifies wandering, or wicked and overly curious men, who, deprived of the light of grace, always wish to learn, and never deserve to arrive at the knowledge of the truth, according to 2 Timothy 3: 'always learning, and never attaining to the knowledge of the truth.'

For this reason such men are called peripatetics, that is, followers of Aristotle, as it were always wandering about among the different schools and masters, but never finding themselves in the discovery of the truth, as a certain Gloss says, in the science below.
Second, as Constantine says, its blood, smeared on the eyelids, does not let hair grow back. For it clogs the pores, and, once they are clogged, hairs do not regrow.
It signifies that the blood of Christ represses the thoughts of the old life from man's understanding, Hebrews 9: 'the blood of Christ will cleanse our conscience from dead works.'
Whoever — Augustine, in the sermon On a Single Martyr: 'whomever the cunning of Satan has bitten, let him look upon Christ hanging on the wood,' and so on.
Third, as the Gloss on Isaiah 2 says, it sucks the oil from lamps, and hides itself in the crevices of walls.

It signifies mercenary clerics and religious who, once they have received their ecclesiastical portion, withdraw themselves from usefulness and common service, and secretly devote themselves to unspeakable deeds.
Of the priest Eli, 1 Kings 2; Ephesians 5: 'the things that are done by them in secret, it is a shame even to speak of.'
Of clerics and monks common in our own time, and especially in the priest who opposed blessed Benedict, of whom blessed Gregory tells in the second book of the Dialogues.
